John 10:20, "He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?" and John 7:20, "The people answered and said, Thou hast a devil." Sometimes they reproached him with being a Samaritan. John 8:48, "Say we not well that thou art a Samaritan and hast a devil?" To be called a Samaritan among the Jews was exceedingly reproachful, for the Samaritans were a people above all others in the world hated by the Jews. He was sometimes charged with being a traitor, and sometimes with being a wicked blasphemer, and one who deserved death on that account, John 10:33. Sometimes they charged him with being a wizard, and one that

-- 198 --

wrought wonders by the help of the devil. They often, when they saw his miracles, were wont to say that he did what he did by the power of Beelzebub. Yea, they called him a devil himself. Matthew 10:25, "If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more shall they call them of his household?" And such was their spite against him that they had agreed to excommunicate, or cast out of the synagogue, any man who owned that he was the Christ, John 9:22. They hated him with a mortal hatred, and wished he was dead, and from time to time intended and endeavored to murder him; yea, were almost always contriving and endeavoring to imbrue their hands in his blood. The life of Christ was an eyesore8 to them. They hated him so that they could not bear that he should live, Psalms 41:5. We very often read of their seeking to kill him, John 5:16; and again ver. John 5:18, and again ch. John 7:25, and ver. John 7:30–32 and John 7:45, and so ch. John 8:22, and Matthew 21:46, and John 10:39. And what pains did many of them take to trap and ensnare him in his words, that they might have something to accuse him of, and so have him put to death. How many snares did they lay for his life, combining together companies of them at one time, the Pharisees and the Sadducees trying their skill. They often actually took up stones to stone him, and once led him to the brow of an hill intending to throw him down, and dash him in pieces.

Christ meekly bore all those injuries from men, he reviled not again; with a lamblike quietness of spirit he passed through all, and at last when he was most injuriously dealt with of all, when his enemies apprehended him and led him as a sheep to the slaughter, [still he was dumb];9 he was a lamb, so he opened not his mouth; no appearance of bitterness or heat of spirit; no appearance of the calm of his mind being disturbed, or any desire of revenge. But he prayed for his crucifiers,1 that they might be forgiven, even when they were nailing him to the cross; yea, did not only pray, but pleaded; he pleaded that they knew not what they did.

Second. If we are not disposed meekly to bear injuries, we are not fitted to live in such a world as this, for we can expect no other than to meet with many injuries in this world. We do not live in heaven, or a world of purity, innocence and love. We dwell in a fallen, corrupt, miserable, wicked world; a world that is very much under the reign and dominion of sin. That principle of divine love, which was at first in the heart of

-- 199 --

man, is extinguished, and revived in but few, and in them but in a very imperfect degree. But those principles which tend to malice and injuriousness are the principles under whose power are the generality of the world. This world is a world where thousands and millions of devils have their range, and where the devil has his dominion; for he is called the god of this world [2 Corinthians 4:4]. All men have not faith, as the Apostle says, 2 Thessalonians 3:2. And indeed, but very few have.

This world has ever been full of unreasonable men, men who will not be governed by rules of justice, but are carried on in that way in which their headstrong lusts drive them. When Christ was about to send his disciples out into the world, he told them, "I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves," Matthew 10:16. And therefore those who have not a spirit with meekness and calmness, and composedness of spirit to bear injuries in such a world are miserable indeed, and are like to be miserable; they are not at all fitted to live in and go through such a world as this is. If every injury with which we meet, every reproach, every spiteful and unjust deed, must put our minds into a rustle2 and tumult, and disturb its calm and peace, that is the way never to enjoy ourselves or have the possession of ourselves, but to be kept in a perpetual turmoil and tumult like a bark that is continually driven to and fro on the stormy ocean. Men who have their spirits heated and enraged, and rising in bitter resentment when they are injured, or unreasonably dealt with, act as if they thought some strange thing had happened to them. Whereas they are very foolish in taking it so, it is no strange thing at all; it is no other than what is to be expected in such a world. Men therefore do not act wisely who have their spirits ruffled by injuries with which they meet. A wise man does not expect any other and is prepared for it, and composes his spirit to bear it.

Third. In this way we shall be most above injuries. He who has such a disposition and frame of mind established that the injuries he receives from men do not exasperate his spirit, or disturb the calm of his mind, lives as it were above injuries, and out of their reach. He conquers them and rides over them, as one that is exalted above them. A man who has so much the exercise of a Christian spirit as to be able meekly to bear all injuries does as it were dwell on high, where his enemies can see him, and show their spite to him, but cannot reach him to disturb him. History gives an account that when the Medes and Persians besieged Babylon the walls of the city were so great, and so exceedingly high, that the

-- 200 --

Babylonians used to stand upon the top of their walls and laugh at their enemies. So one whose soul3 is fortified with a spirit of Christian meekness and a disposition meekly to bear all injuries may, as it were, laugh at the power of the enemy. If any who have an ill spirit against us, and are therefore disposed to do us an injury by reproaching us or otherwise, if by their injuries they see they disturb and vex our minds, they are gratified by it. But if they see that by all they can do they cannot interrupt the calm of our minds, but that we still maintain the same serenity and composed frame, they are frustrated and their end is lost, like a man that shoots an arrow at one that is mounted aloft on eagle's wings beyond his reach; his arrow spends its force before it reaches him, and returns again without doing any execution. So much as a man has his mind disturbed and embittered by the injuries received from an adversary, so much is he afflicted, so much does he appear to fall under the power of his enemy. But if he bears it with an unconquerable meekness, therein he appears above his power. And therefore,

Fourth. This spirit of Christian long-suffering and meekly to bear injuries is a true greatness of soul. It shows a fine and noble valor4 for persons thus to maintain the calm of their minds; it shows an excellent inward fortitude and strength, as Solomon says, Proverbs 16:32, "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." That is, he shows a more noble and excellent valor and greatness of mind than great conquerors who subdue walled cities. It is from a littleness of mind that the soul is easily disturbed, and put out of frame by the reproaches and ill treatment of men, as we see that little streams of water are much disturbed by small unevenness and obstacles with which they meet in their course, and make a great deal of noise as they pass over them; whereas great and mighty streams would pass over such obstacles calmly and quietly, without at all rippling5 the surface of the water. He that possesses his mind after such a manner that when others reproach him and injure him, and show a spiteful spirit towards him, can notwithstanding maintain in calmness a hearty good will to his injurer, and look down on him with real pity for him without any [tumult] or bitterness: he herein as it were manifests a godlike greatness of

-- 201 --

soul. How6 high is such a person's mind exalted? There is no man in the world so much above his adversaries as he; like the sun that is so high that it is not at all disturbed by the storms that are here in this lower world, but goes on in its brightness just as it did before; and like the moon walking in her brightness, while the dogs are barking at her she is not moved, but goes on in her own course placidly shining through the heavens still.

If there be a man of mean outward condition, poor and low in the world, who is very much injured by some great man, as often it has been so that poor Christians have been persecuted by kings and emperors; if he is enabled in Christian meekness and calmness and love to bear it, the poor man in this has vastly the ascendant of his adversary. Beggars in this way are exalted above kings, and giving such a spirit is one way in which God lifts the poor out of the dust, and the beggar from the dunghill, and sets them among princes, and makes them to inherit the throne of glory. Such a meek, quiet, long-suffering spirit shows a true greatness of soul, as it shows wisdom. Such persons show themselves to be wise persons. James 3:13, "Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? Let him show out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom." The wise Solomon, who well knew what belonged to wisdom, is often speaking of the wisdom of such a spirit. Proverbs 13:10, "Only by pride cometh contention: but with the well advised is wisdom." And so ch. Proverbs 29:8, "Wise men turn away wrath." And again Proverbs 19:11, "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; [and it is his glory to pass over a transgression]." On the contrary those who are apt highly to resent injuries, and to be greatly vexed by them, are spoken of in Scripture as of a little, foolish spirit. Proverbs 14:29, "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly." And Ecclesiastes 7:8–9, "The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. For anger resteth in the bosom of fools." And Proverbs 14:16–18, "The fool rageth. He that is soon angry dealeth foolishly: and a man of wicked devices is hated. The simple inherit folly." This meek spirit is spoken of in Scripture as an honorable spirit. Proverbs 20:3, "It is an honor to a man to cease from strife."

Fifth. I would mention the examples of the saints of whom we have an account. Though the example of Christ alone might be sufficient, being the example of the person who is our Head, our Lord and Master, whose followers we all profess to be, and his example a perfect example; yet

-- 202 --

some may be ready to say with regard to the example of Christ that he had no corruption in his heart, and that it cannot be expected of them that they should do as he did. Though this be no reasonable objection, yet the examples of saints that are men of like passions with ourselves are not without their special use, and may in some respects have a peculiar influence. There have been many of these who have set bright examples of this long-suffering, which has been recommended.

One which I shall mention is of David. With what meekness did he bear the injurious treatment which he received from Saul?— when he hunted him as a partridge in the mountain, and pursued him with a most unreasonable envy and malice, and murderous design, who had ever behaved himself dutifully towards him. And when he had opportunity put into his hands of cutting him off, and at once delivering himself from him, and others would have been ready to think it very lawful and commendable to take such an opportunity in their own defense to kill one who sought their lives; yet Saul being the Lord's anointed he chose rather to commit himself still to God, and venture his life in his hands, Saul being yet suffered to live. And when after this he saw that his goodness did not overcome Saul, but that he still pursued him, and David's life seemed to be in imminent danger,7 [[and when again he had the opportunity of destroying him, he chose rather to go out as a wanderer and an outcast, than to injure the one that would have destroyed him]].

Another instance is that of Joseph, the betrothed husband of Mary the mother of Jesus, under a supposed injury from her, though it was no real injury, yet it was the same trial to him as if it had been real. The instance to which I have respect, is that of which we have an account in Matthew 1:18–19, "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost. Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a public example, was minded to put her away privily." Mary was espoused to Joseph, was bound to him by a solemn contract, a contract to be his wife; and after this he perceived that she was with child before they came together, and concluded she had been false and treacherous to him, and had been guilty of adultery; for a carnal commerce with another man in such a case was adultery by the law of Moses, and was to be punished with death, as you may

-- 203 --

see. This, if it had been as he supposed, would have been an injury of that sort which of all others is wont most to provoke and exasperate men. Solomon testifies that jealousy is cruel as the grave [Canticles 8:6]. And again he says, Proverbs 6:34–35, "Jealousy is the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance. He will not regard any ransom; neither will he rest content, although thou givest many gifts." But Joseph being a just man, and a right man of a right spirit, it did not put him into a rage; he was inclined to spare Mary, and not to make it a day of vengeance. Though he chose to put her away and to have nothing further to do with her, yet he was careful out of good will and tenderness to her, though he did not desire she should be his, that she should not be made a public example; and therefore was contriving to keep the matter private, which was a remarkable instance of that of which I have been speaking. Most other men would not have been much concerned about keeping the matter private in such a case as Joseph supposed this to be, nor thought themselves obliged to trouble themselves about the ill consequence of it being known of her8 that had been so false to him; but would have been ready to have said, let her take the consequence of her own abominable treachery and lewdness.

Another example which I shall mention is that of Stephen, of whom we are told, Acts 7:59–60, that when his persecutors were venting their rage upon him by stoning him to death, that he kneeled down and cried with a loud voice, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." This prayer is mentioned as that which he made with his expiring breath, and as the last words which he spoke after his saying, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit"; and immediately upon his making this prayer for his persecutors, he fell asleep.

Another example which I would mention is that of the apostle Paul, who was the subject of numberless injuries from wicked and unreasonable men. He gives some account of his manner of behavior under injuries in 1 Corinthians 4:11–13. "Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwelling place; and labor working with our hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it; being defamed, we entreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day." And many instances there are in human histories of a very remarkable behavior of martyrs and other Christians under unreasonable treatment which they have received from men.

Sixth. And lastly. This is the way to be rewarded with the exercise of

-- 204 --

divine long-suffering towards us. We are often informed in Scripture that we are like to be dealt with of God hereafter according to our own way of dealing with others. There we are told that with the merciful, God will show himself merciful, and that with the froward God will show himself froward, Psalms 18:25–26; and that with what measure we mete, it shall be measured to us again, Matthew 7:2. And in the foregoing chapter, ver. Matthew 7:14–15, Christ tells us that if we forgive men their trespasses our Heavenly Father will also forgive us. But if we forgive not men their trespasses, neither will our Heavenly Father forgive our trespasses. By trespasses here is meant the same as injuries done us. So if we do not bear with men's injuries, neither will our Heavenly Father bear with our injuries. If we do not exercise long-suffering towards men, we cannot expect that God will exercise long-suffering towards us.

But let us consider how greatly we stand in need of God's long-suffering with regard to our injuries towards him. How often and how greatly are we injuriously behaving ourselves towards God; how ill is our treatment of him every day? And if God does not bear with us, and exercise wonderful long-suffering towards us, how miserable shall we be? What will become of us? Let these considerations, therefore, influence all of us to seek such an excellent spirit as that which has been spoken of, and to disallow and suppress everything of the contrary spirit or practice. It would be of an happy influence in our towns and public societies in the management of all our public affairs if such a spirit as this prevailed. It would prevent contention and strife, and so would prevent a great deal of confusion with every evil work. Our affairs would all be carried on without any fierceness, without rage and bitterness of spirit, without harsh and opprobrious expressions to others, and malignant backbiting and contemptuous speeches behind others' backs; and nothing would be lost by it.

Persons' hearts are full of objections against such a meek and quiet bearing of injuries as has been spoken of, some of which I would briefly mention, and answer. As particularly,

Obj. 1. Some may be ready to say that the injuries they receive from men are intolerable; that as the other person has been so unreasonable in what he has said or done, it is so unjust and injurious and ungrateful and the like, that it is more than flesh and blood can bear. They are treated with so much injustice that it is enough to provoke a stone; or they are treated with such contempt that they are nearly trampled upon, and if you tread upon a worm it will turn. In answer to this I would ask the objector a few questions.

-- 205 --

Ques. 1 Whether he thinks the injuries he has received are more intolerable than those which he has offered to God? whether they are more base, unreasonable, ungrateful, aggravated, and heinous; more in number or on any account whatsoever more provoking?

Quest. 2 Do you not hope that God hitherto has or will bear with all this, and notwithstanding all, exercise infinite love and favor? Christ beheld you as such an injurious enemy and9 [he in his righteousness could not stand the] sight of it, and yet notwithstanding maintained a dying love towards you. Has not God long forborne to punish, and do you not hope that he either has or will blot out all your sins, and bestow converting grace, and make you his child?

Ques. 3 When you hope for such long-suffering of God do you not approve of it? think well of it, that it is worthy and excellent, something glorious? Do you not approve of it that Christ should die for such an one, that God should bear with you? or do you disapprove of it? Would you like God better if he should not bear with you?

Ques. 4 If it be excellent and worthy to be approved of in God, why is it not worthy to be imitated by you? or is God more bound to forgive injuries, or is it less heinous to offend the Lord of life and glory than you, a worm? Is it well that you should be forgiven, worthy for you to beg earnestly for [[pardon]], but not worthy for God to desire that you should do so to your fellow creatures?1

Ques. 5 Would you be willing that for time to come God should not bear injuries that are so heinous? Or will you go and tell God that if ever you did so intolerably you would not have him bear with you?

Ques. 6 Did Christ2 [[turn again upon those who injured, and insulted, and trod on him when he was here below; and was he not injured far more grievously than ever you have been?]] Was not Jesus Christ trampled on and trod underfoot a thousand times more than ever you was? Did he turn again? Did you never tread underfoot the Son of God more than you was ever trodden? And is it a more provoking thing for men to tread on you than for you to tread on Christ?

Obj. 2. Those who have injured me persist in it and do not at all repent, but go on still.

Ans. 1. What opportunity could there be for suffering long if it was not

-- 206 --

persisted in long? If it ceases to be persisted in, there ceases to be any further occasion for bearing and suffering.

Ans. 2. Has not God borne with you when you persisted? When he exhorted you, counseled and warned you, you was obstinate, stiff-necked, perverse, and long stood out, as inflexible as a brazen pillar.

Obj. 3. My injurers will be encouraged to go on, and I shall expose myself to be injured more.

Ans. 1. One end of civil government is to provide for the defense of men's just rights.3

Ans. 2. God will undertake to plead your cause, and he is more able to put a stop to the injuries offered you than you. He hath said, Vengeance is mine, I will repay [Romans 12:19]. So God undertook for David. If you undertake, God will leave it with you. Proverbs 24:17–18, "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth: lest the Lord see it, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him."

Ans. 3. If they should be encouraged to go on, would your making such an improvement of God's forbearance put a stop to it?

Ans. 4. When once such a method puts a stop to injuries, it has a contrary4 [later effect.] [[And in the observation and experience of men, it is generally found that a meek and long-suffering spirit puts an end to injuries, while a revengeful spirit does but provoke them.]] Romans 12:19–20, "Avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. Therefore, if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head."5

-- 207 --

II. I come now secondly to show that a Christian spirit disposes persons freely to do good to others. In speaking to this point I would, first, briefly open the nature of the duty of doing good to others; second, show how that a Christian spirit will dispose persons to this.

First. I would briefly open the nature of the duty here spoken of; and here three things are to be considered, viz. first, the act, viz. doing good to others; second, the objects, or to whom we should do good; third, the manner of doing, viz. freely.

1. The act, which is the matter of the duty, which is doing good to others. There are many ways in which persons may do good to others, and in which they are obliged so to do as they have opportunity.

(1) Persons may do good to others' souls, which is the most excellent way of doing good. Men may be and oftentimes are the instruments of spiritual and eternal good to others; and wherein any are so, they are instruments of greater good to them than if they were instruments of their being possessed of all the riches of the world. Men may do good to others' souls by taking pains to instruct the ignorant and lead them into the knowledge of the great things of religion, and by counseling and warning others and stirring them up to their duty, and to a seasonable and thorough care of their soul's welfare; or by Christian reproof of others who wander out of the way of their duty; and also by setting them good examples, which is a thing the most needful of all and commonly the most effectual of any for promoting the good of others' souls. This must accompany those other means of doing good to others' souls, of instructing, counseling, warning and reproving, and is needful to give force to those means and to make them take effect. It is the most likely thing to render them effectual of anything whatsoever. And whatever warnings and reproofs are given without an answerable example, they will not be very likely to take effect.

Men may do good to the souls of vicious persons by being the instruments of reclaiming them from their vicious courses. They may do good to the souls of secure and senseless sinners by putting them in mind of

-- 208 --

their misery and danger and so being the instruments of awakening them. And persons may be the instruments of others' conversion,6 of bringing them home to Christ. We read in Daniel 12:3 of those that turn many to righteousness. And the saints may be the instruments of comforting and establishing one another, and strengthening one another in faith and obedience, of quickening and enlivening one another, of rousing one another out of dull and dead forms, and helping one another under temptations, and directing one another in doubtful and intricate cases, and of comforting one another under darkness, and greatly promoting each other's spiritual joy, and so edifying one another.

(2) Persons may do good to others as they are the means of their outward good. They may help others under their external calamities and difficulties. There are innumerable kinds of temporal calamities to which men are liable in which they may stand in need of the help of their neighbors. Various kinds are mentioned in Matthew 25:35–36, "I was an hungered, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me." Persons may do good to others by furthering their outward estate or substance, or with regard to their good name, or their esteem and acceptance among men, or otherwise may greatly contribute to the comfortableness of others' circumstances in the world. Persons by their doing good to others externally are under the greater advantages to do good to others' souls. When their counsels, and warnings, and instructions, and good examples are accompanied with outward kindness, it tends to open the way for the effect of instructions and good examples, and to give force to them to win and draw them to a due regard to them wherein they seek their spiritual good.

Persons may thus contribute to others' good in three ways, viz. first, by giving to them, by bestowing on them those things which we have and which they need, or which may be to their benefit; second, by doing for them, by taking pains for them to help them or promote their welfare. Or third, by suffering for them, by bearing their burdens for them, or at least in part that we may make their burdens the lighter. In each of these ways Christianity requires us to do good to others. It requires us to give to others, Luke 6:38, "Give, and it shall be given unto you." It requires us to do for others, and to labor and spend time for them. 1 Thessalonians 2:9, "For ye remember, brethren, our labor and travail; for laboring night

-- 209 --

and day, because we would not be chargeable to any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God." Hebrews 6:10, "For God is not unrighteous to forget your work of faith and labor of love." It requires us to suffer for others. Galatians 6:2, "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." 1 John 3:16, "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren." So much may suffice [in] the matter of this duty, or the act of doing good to others. I come now

2. To speak of the object of this act, or to show who those are to whom we should do good. The object of this act is often expressed in Scripture by that word, our "neighbor"; for this duty is implied in that command of loving our neighbor as ourselves. But then perhaps some will be ready to ask as the lawyer did, who asked Christ what he should do that he might inherit eternal life; and when Christ directed him to love the Lord his God with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his mind, and his neighbor as himself, [asked]7 who was his neighbor? And we have the answer given in Christ's answer to him; viz. Luke 10:29–37, "But he, willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbor? And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead. And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. And likewise a Levite, when he was at the place, came and looked on him, and passed by on the other side. But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him, and went to him, and bound his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee. Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbor unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, he that showed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise."8

Christ led the lawyer by this to own that the Samaritan was neighbor to him that fell among thieves, and in doing as he did to the Jew to fulfill

-- 210 --

the law of loving his neighbor as himself, though the Jews and Samaritans were bitter enemies one to another, and there was the greatest national enmity between them. And it necessarily followed that if the Samaritan was neighbor to the Jew, his enemy, so the Jew was neighbor to the Samaritan; because neighborhood is a mutual relation equally predicable of both those between whom there is such a relation. The Samaritans and Jews were looked upon by each other as wicked, vile and accursed, and were bitter enemies one to another. And therefore it may be shown who they are to whom we should do good in three things.

(1) We should do good to both good and bad. This we should do as we would imitate God, our Heavenly Father. Matthew 5:45, "That ye may be the children of your Father which is in Heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." The world is full of various kinds of persons; some are good, and some evil. We should especially do good to those that are of the household of faith, or that we have reason charitably to look upon as saints. But though we should more abound in beneficence to them, yet our doing good should not be confined to them; but we should do good to all men. Galatians 6:10, "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith." While we live in this world we see many men of very ill properties and hateful dispositions and practices. Some are very proud men, loose, immoral; some are very covetous, close, hard, unreasonable, profane, despisers of God, unjust. But those and other bad qualities should not hinder our beneficence, or prevent our doing them good as we have opportunity.

(2) We should do good both to friends and enemies. We are obliged to do good to our friends. Besides the obligations which we are under to do good to men as our fellow creatures, and those that are made in the image of God, we are under the obligations of friendship and gratitude. Proverbs 18:24, "A man that hath friends, must show himself friendly." But we are not only obliged to do good to them, but also to our enemies. Matthew 5:43–44, "Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy. But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you and persecute you." We should do good to those that do ill to us. This should be the Christian's way of retaliating, not returning evil for evil but good for evil. Romans 12:17, "Recompense to no man evil for evil." Ver. Romans 12:21, "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." 1 Thessalonians 5:15, "See that none render evil for evil unto any man; but ever follow that which is good among yourselves,

-- 211 --

and to all men." 1 Peter 3:9, "Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing."9

(3) We should do good to the thankful and the unthankful. This we should also do, as we would imitate our Father which is in Heaven. Luke 6:35, "Love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind to the unthankful and to the evil." Many make that an objection against doing good to others, giving anything to others which they need, "If I do, they will never thank me for it; they will not accept it thankfully. If I go on with kindness, they will still go on with their abuses and injuries." And this men are ready to think excuses them from showing any more kindness. But such persons have not sufficiently learned Christ, and [show]1 their unacquaintance with the nature and spirit of Christianity. And thus much for the object of doing good. I come now

3. To speak of the manner in which we should do good to others, which is expressed in this one word "freely." In the proposition which we are upon and implied in the words of the text, to be kind is to have a disposition freely to do good. Whatever good is done, it is no proper kindness in the doer of it unless it be done freely. But our doing good freely implies three things.

(1) That our doing good be not mercenary, that we do not do it as being hired to do it, that we do not do it for the sake of any reward received or expected from the person to whom we do it. Luke 6:35, "Do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again." Rich men will oftentimes do good to rich men expecting to receive as much or more again. But we should do good to those that are poor, and can never recompense us. Luke 14:12–14, "When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbors; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompense be made thee. But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: and thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just." That our doing good be

-- 212 --

free and not mercenary, it is necessary that what we do be not for the sake of any temporal gain, or any respect, or only to promote our temporal interest whether of profit or honor.

(2) That our doing good be free it is requisite that we do it cheerfully; that we do it heartily from real good will. What is done heartily is done from love, is done with delight, and not grudgingly, and with backwardness and loathness. 1 Peter 4:9, "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." 2 Corinthians 9:7, "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity; for God loveth a cheerful giver." This is a qualification of our doing for others and giving to them much insisted on in Scripture. Romans 12:8, "He that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that showeth mercy, with cheerfulness." God gives a strict charge that our hearts should not be grieved when we give to our poor brother. Deuteronomy 15:10, "Thou shalt surely give him, and thine heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him."

(3) This implies that we give liberally or bountifully, that we should not be scant or sparing in our gifts, but open-hearted and open-handed. 2 Corinthians 9:11, "Being enriched in everything to all bountifulness." Thus God requires that when we give to the poor we should open our hand wide unto him. Deuteronomy 15:7–8, "If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren within any of thy gates in thy land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother: but thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need in that which he wanteth." We are told that the liberal soul shall be made fat, Proverbs 11:25. The Apostle would have the Corinthians be bountiful in their contributions to their poor brethren in Judea. 2 Corinthians 9:6, "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully." And ver. 2 Corinthians 9:11, "Being enriched in everything to all bountifulness." Having thus explained the nature of this duty of freely doing good to others, I now proceed

Second. To show that a Christian spirit will dispose thus to do good to others, and this appears from these two things.

1. The main thing in that love, which is the sum of the Christian spirit, is benevolence or good will to others. We have heretofore, in speaking from the former verses of this chapter, shown what Christian love is, and how it is variously denominated according to the various objects and exercises of it; and particularly how that, as it respects the good enjoyed or to be enjoyed by the beloved, it is called love of benevolence; and as it

-- 213 --

respects good to be enjoyed in the beloved, it is called love of complacence.2 Love of benevolence is that disposition which a man has who desires or delights in the good of another. And this is the main thing in Christian love, the most essential thing, and that whereby our love is most of an imitation of the eternal love and grace of God, and the dying love of Christ, which consists in benevolence or good will. And therefore the angels at the birth of Christ, as in Luke 2:14, sang, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will towards men." So that the main thing in Christian love is good will, or a spirit to delight in, and seek the good of those who are the objects of that love.

2. The most proper evidence of such a principle's being real and sincere is its being effectual. The proper evidence of wishing good to another is doing good to another. What can be plainer than that the proper evidence of the will is the act? The act of the man follows the will wherein the man has power to act. The proper evidence of a man's sincerely desiring the good of another is seeking it in his3 practice. That which a man sincerely desires he will seek, so far as the thing desired is within his reach. The Scripture therefore speaks of doing good as the proper evidence of love. And therefore loving in deed or practice and loving in truth or reality are put for the same thing in Scripture.4 1 John 3:18–19, "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth. Hereby we know that we are of the truth." That is, hereby we know that we are sincere. James 2:15–16, "If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?"

Application

I. Use may be of reproof. If a Christian spirit disposes persons freely to

-- 214 --

do good to others, all those who are of a contrary spirit and practice may hence be reproved. A malignant, malicious spirit is directly contrary to this; for that is a spirit which disposes men to do evil to others, and not good. And opposite to this, also, is a close selfish spirit whereby men are wholly bent on their own interest, and averse in anything to forego their own interest for the sake of others. And they are of a spirit and practice opposite to this who show an exorbitantly craving spirit, who will take all opportunities to get all they possibly can of their neighbors in their dealings with them, asking more for what they sell to their neighbor or do for him than the thing is worth, squeezing and extorting to the utmost out of him, being unreasonable in their demands, having no regard to the real value of what their neighbor has of them, so much as the advantage they have as it were to force it out of him. And on the contrary, being pinching in things which he buys of his neighbor, or which his neighbor does for him, being very hard and pinching, and backward to give what the thing is really worth. Such a spirit and practice are very unbecoming of Christians, and contrary to the Christian spirit.

II. Use may be of exhortation to this duty of freely doing good to others. Seeing this is a Christian duty, and a virtue becoming the gospel, and what a Christian spirit disposes to, let us all who call ourselves Christians comply with it; let us all as we have opportunity do good to others' souls and bodies. Let us to that end be willing to do, and give, and suffer, and this that we may do good to the evil and the good, to friends and enemies, to the thankful and unthankful; let our benevolence and beneficence be universal, and let us do it freely and without grudging. Here let several things be considered.

First. What a great honor is it to be made an instrument of good in the world. When persons fill up their lives with doing good, God puts that honor upon them as to make them blessings in the world. The same great honor is put upon them which God put upon Abraham. Genesis 12:2, "I will bless thee, and thou shalt be a blessing."

The light of nature teaches this to be a great honor; and therefore formerly the heathen kings and princes used to assume to themselves the titles of benefactors; that is, doers of good, as the most honorable title they could think of. Luke 22:25, "And he said unto them, The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors." And it was a common thing in heathen lands, when those who had done a great deal of good in their lifetime were dead, for the people among whom they dwelt to reckon them among the gods, and to build temples to their honor. So far as God

-- 215 --

makes men the instruments of doing good to others, he makes them like the heavenly bodies, the sun, moon and stars, that by the light they shed abroad in the world are blessings. He hereby makes them like the angels, who are ministering spirits to others' good; yea, he makes them like himself who is the fountain of goodness. It is godlike freely to do good.

Second. For us freely to do good to others is but to do to others as we would that they should to us. If others have a hearty good will to us, and there is a great deal of kindness, and they are ready to help us when we stand in need of help, and to that end are free to do for us, to labor for us, to give to us, to suffer for us, and help bear our burdens, and share with us in our calamities, are free and cheerful in it, and seem to be open-hearted and liberal in it, this we all approve of when we are the objects; this we highly commend; we shall take occasion to speak well of such persons; we are not apt to think that they exceed their duty, but that they do as becomes Christians. Let us therefore consider that if this is so approvable and so much to be commended in others towards us, we ought to do so to others. We should approve of and exemplify it in ourselves. When we think of giving to the poor, we should make it our own case. And

Third. Let us consider how kind God and Christ have been to us, and how much good we have received from them. How much outward kindness have we received, and what great good things hath God bestowed for our spiritual and eternal good! God hath given more than if he had bestowed on us all the kingdoms of the world; he hath given his own Son. God hath not been shorthanded, but exceedingly liberal. Christ has done great things; he hath gone through great labors. And he hath bestowed much upon us. He hath given his own blood. He was rich, and became poor for our sakes [2 Corinthians 8:9]. He hath suffered great things. He did all freely, without grudging, and without hope of reward. What great things hath God done for those of you who are converted and brought home to Christ? And all this have God and Christ done for us when we were not good, but evil; not friends, but enemies, and though very unthankful.

Fourth. Let us consider what great rewards are promised unto those who freely do good to others. God has promised that to the merciful man he will show himself merciful, Psalms 18:25. There is scarce any duty in the whole Bible which has so many promises of reward. We could not desire more or greater promises of reward both in this life and that which is to come. The Scripture teaches that in such cases the giver is the greater gainer. Acts 20:35, "It is more blessed to give than to receive." He who

-- 216 --

gives bountifully is more happy, is a greater gainer by his own bountiful gifts which he parts with, than he that receives this bounty. What is bestowed in doing good to others is not lost, as if a man throws what he had into the sea. But see what Solomon says, Ecclesiastes 11:1, "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days."5 What is so given is lent and committed to a faithful hand, to the Lord, who no doubt will pay. Proverbs 19:17, "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again." He will not only pay, but with great increase. Luke 6:38, "Give, and it shall be given unto you." Scattering thus is the way to increase. Proverbs 11:24, "There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth." Isaiah 32:8, "The liberal diviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand." What natural men do and give in this way, God is wont to reward with great temporal rewards. Proverbs 28:27, "He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack." God is wont as much to prosper men's gifts to the poor as he is to prosper their seed sown in the field. One is as likely to be prospered as the other, as Solomon teaches, Ecclesiastes 11:6, "In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand; for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good." Does the husbandman look on his seed lost, which he sows? 2 Corinthians 9:6–8, "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully. Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work." Many do but little consider how their prosperity depends on providence. "The blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich," Proverbs 10:22. This is the way to have God's help in times of trouble. Psalms 41:1, "Blessed is he that considereth the poor, the Lord will deliver him in time of trouble." If you give in a way of Christian charity, it is the way to lay up treasure in heaven, to have eternal rewards. This is laying up treasures in bags that wax not old, which Christ speaks of, Luke 12:33, "Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves

-- 217 --

bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth." For feeding with some of your bread those that cannot recompense you, you shall be recompensed in the resurrection of the just. Luke 14:13–15, "But when thou makest a feast call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just. And when one of them that sat at meat with him heard these things, he said unto him, Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God." This is the best way of laying up for yourself both for time and eternity, both for yourself and your posterity. Psalms 112:5, "A good man showeth favor and lendeth." Ver. Psalms 112:9, "He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; [his righteousness endureth for ever; his horn shall be exalted with honor]." Ver. Psalms 112:2, "His generation shall be mighty upon earth: [the generation of the upright shall be blessed].6 [[And when Christ shall come to judgment, and all people shall be gathered before him, then to those who were kind and benevolent, in the true spirit of Christian love, to the suffering and the poor, he shall say, Matthew 25:34–36, Matthew 25:40, "Come ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: for I was an hungered, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink; I was a stranger, and ye took me in; naked, and ye clothed me; I was sick, and ye visited me; I was in prison, and ye came unto me." "Verily, I say unto you, inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of those, my brethren, ye have done it unto me."]]

-- 218 --

SERMON FIVE: CHARITY CONTRARY TO AN ENVIOUS SPIRIT
Charity envieth not. I CORINTHIANS 13:4.

I HAVE already explained what precedes in the context, having particularly insisted on each foregoing part of this chapter. The Apostle in the foregoing verses shows the necessity and importance of charity, and in this verse begins particularly to explain the nature of charity in the properties and effects of it. In the preceding part of the verse the Apostle shows the nature and tendency of Christian charity or divine love with respect to evil received from others, and doing good to others. With respect to evil to be received from others charity suffers long, or meekly bears injuries received; with respect to those1 received by others charity is kind, or freely does good to others. In the remaining part of the verse the Apostle shows the nature of charity with respect to good bestowed by others, and good possessed by ourselves; or the good that others have, or that we have.

1. With respect to good or property possessed by others. And with regard to this, the Apostle declared it not to be the nature of charity to envy them the [good]2 which they possess. Charity envieth not.

2. With respect to good that we possess ourselves. The nature of charity is expressed in this, that it vaunteth not itself, and is not puffed up. Men are naturally inclined, when they possess any considerable good or prosperity to vaunt themselves in it, and to be puffed up by it. But a spirit of Christian love is not of this tendency, but the contrary. But it is the former of these that I would now insist on the consideration of, viz. the nature and tendency of charity with regard to what of good or

-- 219 --

prosperity others possess, in that it envieth not others anything which they possess.3 And from the words I would raise this observation, viz.

Doctrine

A truly Christian spirit is opposite to an envious spirit.

In handling this subject I would

I. Show what the nature of an envious spirit is.

II. Show wherein a Christian spirit is contrary to such a spirit.

III. Show the reason and evidence of this doctrine, and then make an application.

I. Show the nature of envy. Envy may be defined, a spirit of opposition to others' comparative happiness, or to the happiness of others considered as compared with their own.4 The thing to which envious persons are opposed is the comparative relation between that state of honor or happiness which others have, or may have, and their own state. This is especially called envy when persons are opposite to the honor or prosperity which others have, because therein they are above them, either that they have in general more prosperity than they or because they have some particular honor and enjoyment which they have not. There is a disposition naturally in man to love to be uppermost, and this disposition is directly crossed when they see others above them. But it is from the same sort of spirit when men are opposite to others' prosperity because of its proportion to their own, or because of its comparative relation to their own state, whether they are above them or not. Thus from the same disposition a person may be opposite to another's being equal to him in happiness or having the same enjoyments as he has. As men very commonly are, they cannot bear that others should rival them or vie with them in honor and prosperity. There is a disposition in men to be singular in happiness; they love to be distinguished in their advancement. Such a spirit is called envy in Scripture. Thus Moses speaks of Joshua's envying for his sake, when Eldad and Medad were admitted to a like privilege with him in having the spirit of prophecy given them. Numbers 11:29, "Enviest thou for my sake? Would God that all the Lord's people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit upon them!"5 Yea, persons from such a spirit may not only be unwilling that

-- 220 --

others should be above them, or equal to them, but also that they should be near them. For that disposition which men have to be distinguished in prosperity and honor is the more gratified by how much they are distinguished; and the more others are below them, the more are they distinguished, the more singular do they appear in their prosperity. And this disposition may be exercised either with respect to the prosperity which others may obtain, or which they have obtained.

First. This spirit or disposition may be exercised either with respect to the prosperity which others may obtain, or are capable of, and so is manifest in a bitterness or unwillingness that they should obtain such prosperity, because if they do they will be in better circumstances than we, or equal to us, or nearer to us than we are willing they should be. This is more commonly called grudging. Or

Second. This spirit may be exercised with respect to the prosperity that others have obtained. They are opposite in their hearts to that prosperity or honor which they see others possessed of. And this opposition is manifest in two things.

1. In an uneasiness in seeing others' prosperity instead of rejoicing in it. It is a trouble to them. It is grievous to their spirits to see them rising so high, and come to such honor and prosperity.6 It is no comfortable news

-- 221 --

to them to hear of their having obtained such and such advantages or honors, and it is uncomfortable to them to see it. And from such a spirit they stand ready to rejoice at anything which happens to diminish the honor and comfort of what they have obtained; they would be glad to have them brought down. And oftentimes they show this uneasiness by endeavors of one kind or other to bring them down. If they have an opportunity put into their hands to pull them down, they will embrace it. And it is from this disposition that seeing others' prosperity often sets persons talking against them and speaking evil of them. They envy them the prosperity or honor they have obtained, and they hope by speaking evil of them in some measure to diminish that honor and to beget a mean opinion in others of them.

2. This opposition to their prosperity appears in a dislike of their persons for it. By seeing how they prosper and to what honor they attain they grow into a distaste and disrelish of them. Persons often have an ill spirit against others for nothing else but their prosperity. That is their crime for which their spirits are embittered against them. They resent their prospering and coming to honor as if they were guilty of some injury to them in it; and sometimes there is a settled hatred in some towards others upon this account. So Joseph's brethren hated him on account of the love their father had to him above them, and on account of his doing more for him than for them.7 But this may suffice concerning the nature of envy. I now proceed

II. To show wherein a Christian spirit is contrary to such a spirit; and

First. A Christian spirit disallows of the exercises and expressions of such a spirit. He who is influenced in the course of his life and actions by Christian principles, though he has envy as well as other corruptions in his heart, yet he abhors such a spirit as being very unbecoming of him as a Christian, and contrary to the nature and will of God. He sees it to be

-- 222 --

an odious spirit; he does not only see the odiousness of it as it is in others, but as it is in him. And therefore when he sees the exercise of such a spirit rising in him on any occasion, so far as he is influenced by a Christian spirit he will be alarmed at it, and will fight against it, and will not allow of it, and will by no means suffer his envious spirit to break forth and show itself in words or actions; he will be ashamed and grieved at what he sees of it in his heart, and will cross8 the hateful disposition he feels in him and will go contrary to it in his outward practice.

Second. It mortifies such a principle or disposition in the heart. It does not only oppose the exercises of such a spirit and oppose the outward expressions of it, but so far as a Christian spirit prevails it mortifies and subdues such a principle itself in the heart. So that a man in that proportion shall cease to feel an inclination to grudge another any property which he might obtain, or to be grieved at that which they have obtained; much less to dislike him, or entertain any ill will against him for it. A Christian spirit disposes persons to feel contentment with their own condition, and with that share which God has given them among their neighbors, and to a quietness of spirit with regard to the [[allotments]] and distributions which God in his providence makes of good things to himself and others, as the Apostle says, Philippians 4:11–12, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: everywhere and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need."

Third. A Christian spirit disposes persons to rejoice in others' prosperity. It not only mortifies a disposition to grieve at it, but on the contrary gives a disposition to rejoice in it. A Christian spirit disposes to a compliance with that rule, Romans 12:15, "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." I proceed now

III. To show the reason and evidence of this, or to show that it is so, and why it is so that a Christian spirit is thus opposite to a spirit of envy, which may appear by considering these three things. First, how much a spirit and practice contrary to this is insisted on in the precepts which Christ hath given. Second, how much the history and doctrine of the gospel hold forth to embrace those precepts. And third, how a spirit of love will dispose to yield to the authority of those precepts, and to the influence of those enforcements.

First. If we consider how much a spirit and practice which are contrary

-- 223 --

to a spirit of envy is insisted on in the precepts which Christ hath given. How full is the New Testament of precepts of good will to others, principles of meekness, humility and beneficence, which are all opposite to a spirit of envy! And how often are we particularly warned there against envy. Romans 13:13, "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in strife and envying."9 The same Apostle [[blames]] the Corinthians as being carnal, because there was envying among them. 1 Corinthians 3:3, "Ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal?" So the same Apostle mentions his fears concerning the Corinthians, lest he should find envy among them. 2 Corinthians 12:20, "I fear lest when I come I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, etc."1 And envy is banded among other works of the flesh, Galatians 5:19–21, "Now the works of the flesh are manifest"; and then follows a catalogue of them, and among them are mentioned hatred, variance, wrath, strife, seditions, envyings. And the same Apostle warns them against it, ver. Galatians 5:26, "Let us not be desirous of vainglory, provoking one another, envying one another." Again envy is condemned, 1 Timothy 6:4–6, "Doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings, etc."2 And envy is mentioned by the Apostle as one of those things that the Christians lived in before their conversion but were now redeemed from, and therefore counsels them to forsake it. Tit 3:3, "For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another." So the apostle James speaks of envy as exceedingly contrary to Christianity and all that is good. James 3:14–16, "But if ye have bitter envying and strife in your hearts, glory not, and lie not against the truth. This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish. For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work." And he warns against this, ch. James 5:9, "Grudge not one against another, brethren, lest ye be condemned; behold, the judge standeth before the door." So the apostle Peter warns against the same, 1 Peter 2:1–2, "Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all

-- 224 --

evil speakings. As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby." Thus the New Testament of Jesus Christ is full of precepts which are opposite to a spirit of envy.

Second. Let it be considered how much the doctrines and history of the gospel hold forth to enforce those precepts.

I. If we consider the Christian scheme of doctrine, it tends greatly to enforce these precepts. The gospel scheme, all of it from beginning to end, tends to the contrary of this spirit. The Christian form of doctrine doth abundantly hold forth those things which militate against a spirit of envy. The things which they teach us of God are exceedingly contrary to it. For there we are taught how far God was from grudging us the most exceeding honor and blessedness, and how he has grudged us nothing as too much to be done for us, and nothing as too great and too good to be given us; he hath not grudged us his only begotten Son, that which was most precious and most dear of all to himself; for what was dearer to God than his only begotten, dearly beloved Son? He hath not grudged us the highest honor and blessedness in union with him. The doctrines of the gospel teach us how far Jesus Christ was from grudging us anything which he could do for or give to us. He did not grudge us a life spent in labor and suffering; he did not grudge us his own precious blood; he hath not grudged us a sitting with him on his throne in heaven, and being partakers with him of that heavenly kingdom and glory which the Father hath given him, and sitting with him on thrones judging the world, though we deserve to be had in infinite contempt and abhorrence by him. The Christian scheme of doctrine teaches us how Christ came into the world to deliver us from the fruits of Satan's envy towards us. The devil being miserable himself envied mankind that happiness which they had, and couid not bear to see our first parents in their happy state in Eden, and therefore exerted himself to the utmost to ruin them, and accomplished it. The gospel teaches how Christ came into the world to destroy the works of the devil, and deliver us from that misery into which his envy has brought us.3

-- 225 --

2. If we consider what we are informed of in the history of the gospel, it tends greatly to enforce those precepts which are opposite to envy, and particularly the history of the life of Christ and the example which he hath set us. How far was he from a spirit of envy? How contented in his mean and low and afflicted circumstances, how far did he appear from envying those that were possessed of worldly wealth and honor, or coveting their circumstances; he rather chose to continue in his outward meanness. And when the multitude were filled with admiration of him on occasion of his doctrine and miracles, and seemed to stand ready to make him a king, he refused that earthly honor which they intended to put upon him, and withdrew himself to be out of their way, as you may see in the sixth chapter of John, ver. John 6:15. And when John the Baptist was so greatly honored by the people as a great prophet, and all Judea and Jerusalem went out to him to hear him and be baptized of him, while he yet remained in obscurity Christ envied him not, but himself went out among others to be baptized of him in Jordan. Though he was John's Lord and Master, and he, the latchet of whose shoes he was not worthy to unloose, and to whom John had more need to come to be baptized of him as he himself testifies; yet he refused not to contribute to that honor which John had among men, which for the present was far greater than that which Christ had. And how far was he from grudging his disciples any honor or privilege as too great for them, who told them and promised them, that after his death and ascension they should do greater works than he had done, John 14:12, that they should have greater success than he had had in preaching the gospel; for how few followers

-- 226 --

had Christ? But after his ascension what multitudes? Such things do the doctrines and history of the gospel hold forth to enforce those precepts of Christ which forbid envy.

Third. Let it be considered how that love or charity, which is the sum of the Christian spirit, will dispose to yield to the authority of those precepts, and to the influence of those enforcements. A spirit of love disposes to this either, first, directly by its own immediate tendency, or second, mediately, as it works by humility.

1. Christian love disposes to hearken to those precepts which forbid envy, and to the gospel motives to it, by its own immediate tendency. The nature of Christian love to men is directly contrary to envy. For love does not grieve but rejoices at the good of the beloved. And surely love to our neighbor does not dispose to hate our neighbor for his prosperity; for that would be a great absurdity. And love to God also has a direct tendency to influence a person to obey his commands. The natural, genuine fruit of love to God is obedience; and therefore it will tend to obedience to those commands wherein he forbids envy as well as others,4 and to them more especially; for love delights to obey no commands so much as those which require love. And so love to God will dispose to follow God's example wherein he hath been so far from grudging us anything which we are capable of enjoying. And love to Christ will dispose us to imitate him in that which is so contrary to envy as his not grudging his own blood, and the examples he hath set us in the course of his life in this world.

2. A spirit of Christian love disposes to this more mediately, viz. by working by humility. It is pride that is the great root and source of envy. It is because of the pride of men's hearts that they have such a disposition to be distinguished and singular in honor and prosperity, and making them so uneasy at seeing others above them. But a spirit of love tends to mortify pride and to work humility in the heart. Love to God tends to this, as it implies a sense of God's infinite excellency, and therefore tends to a sense of our own comparative meanness and unworthiness. And love to men tends to an humble behavior among men, as it disposes men to acknowledge the excellencies of others and the honor due to them, and to an esteeming others better than ourselves. But because I shall have occasion more particularly to show how Christian love tends to humility in speaking to the words which next follow the text, if God give opportunity, I shall say no more of it at present, but hasten to the

-- 227 --

Application

In two uses: first, of self-examination; second, of exhortation.

I. Of self-examination. Let this put us all upon examining ourselves with respect to this hateful spirit, even a spirit of envy to which we have heard a Christian spirit is so contrary. Let us examine ourselves as to time past; let us look over our past behavior among men. We have many of us long been members of human society, and have lived by others, and have had to do with them in many ways, and on many occasions, as being concerned with them both in public and private affairs. And we have seen others in prosperity, and it may be prospering in their affairs more than we; they have had more of the world, and have lived in greater fullness and ease and with more comfortable accommodations than we. We have perhaps seen and lived by others in much more honorable circumstances than ourselves. And possibly some others whom heretofore we used to look upon as our equals, with whom we used to be mates, and used to look upon ourselves and others used to look upon us as good men as they; yea, it may be formerly we were above them, but after that we have seen them rise above us, they have grown in wealth faster than we, and we have seen them promoted and advanced, while we have been left behind and now see them in a station much superior to us. It may be there have been such trials time after time through a great part of the course of our lives.

Now let us inquire how these things have wrought with us; how have our hearts stood, and how has been our behavior in these circumstances? Has there not been a great deal of envy, uneasiness and sorrow at it? Has it not been an uncomfortable sight to us; has not our neighbors' success been uncomfortable news? Have we not wished to see them brought down, and glad to hear of anything to eclipse their honor? Have we not been forward to do something to lessen their honor, or to speak ill of them? Have we not been forward to take opportunities when we thought we had an opportunity to lessen their prosperity or honor in any respect? Have we not had embittered spirits towards them and been the more ready to look upon them with an evil eye on this account? Have we not been more forward on this account to oppose them in public affairs, and to be stiff and willful in opposing their interest?5 Have we not been more ready to be in a heat of spirit, and to talk in any public or private conversation wherein we have been concerned with them with [envy of

-- 228 --

their prosperity]?6 When we look back on our past lives, can we not see that a considerable part of our lives has been spent in envying others, and many of our days with envy burning in our hearts towards one another?

And how is it now? Be strict in searching your hearts for the present. Do you not really at this day carry old envious grudging in your heart against this and that man, whom you see from Sabbath to Sabbath sitting with you in the meeting house, and from time to time sitting with you at the Lord's table? Is not the prosperity of those and those persons7 now really an eyesore to you, and one thing which makes your life more uncomfortable? Should you not think your life more comfortable if such and such men were brought down? Would it not be gratifying to your inclination? Would there not be an inward pleasedness and gladness in it? And are you not now often an occasion, from such a spirit as this, of speaking evil, contemptuously, and with a kind of indignation to others who seem to be with you in this opposition?

Let those who are above others in prosperity inquire whether they do not exercise an evil spirit of opposition to others' comparative happiness. Is there not a disposition in you to pride yourself in your being so much above them, and an opposition to their prospering in the world, lest they should come to be equal with you, a spirit to grudge them prosperity as being too good for them, and from thence a disposition to bear others down and to keep them down to your utmost? Such as thus show envy towards others when they are above them, if they had the temptation which others have, would show as much and probably much more envy. Very likely if you find such things as these you justify yourself, and do not call them envy, but give some other name to them.

Men are wont to have various excuses for their envious spirit by which they account themselves justifiable. I would mention two.

First. Some are ready to say of others that they are not worthy of their honor and prosperity which they have; they are not fit for it; they are a very ill set of men; they are not half so worthy of that honor and advancement which they have as many others of their neighbors whom they are above. And where is the man in the world who envies another for his honor or prosperity but what thinks they are not worthy of that prosperity and honor which they grudge them? Did Joseph's brethren think

-- 229 --

[[him worthy of the peculiar love of his father]]?8 Did the Jews think the Gentiles worthy of the privileges when they were so filled with envy towards them for their being admitted to them, Acts 13:45 and Acts 17:5? It is generally so that when others are promoted to honor, or in any respect come to remarkable prosperity, for others to take that occasion to tell of their faults and crimes, and set forth their unworthiness; all then is reckoned up. Whereas it is their prosperity and their own envy of them for it which dispose them to think of their faults. Here I would desire such persons as think that they are to be justified in being opposite to the prosperity of others because they are unworthy or unfit to enjoy them, I say I would desire such to inquire diligently which hurts them most, their faults or their prosperity. If their faults hurt you most, if that be the chief thing which grieves you, you would be grieved at them whether they were in prosperity or not. If it is their faults which are really what grieve you, then you are grieved for their calamity and not their prosperity; for their faults are their calamity. You are hurt and inwardly grieved with compassion that they suffer such calamity.

Second. Another excuse which some make for being opposite to the honor and prosperity of others is that they make a bad use of them, that they lift them up, that they cannot bear them, they do not know how to manage them, they improve them very ill, they are insufferable and scornful; there is no doing with them under their prosperity, it is fit they should be brought down, it is best for them that they should be without their prosperity, it would tend to humble them, the best service any can do them is to pull them down, to bring them down to that place which is fit for them. But here strictly inquire whether you do indeed lament the hurt which their prosperity does them out of pity, or is it out of envy? If you dislike it because it does them hurt and is not best for them, if it be indeed so that it is pity, and that which you grieve at is their calamity, and not their prosperity; you love them, and so are out of sincere love

-- 230 --

heartily sorry for their calamity; you have a compassion of heart towards them that they are so far from prosperity, that they have got into a snare. Is it so or not? Do not deceive yourself. Is it as their calamity that you are hurt for them? Or is it not really as their prosperity that you are hurt for yourself, that you are left so much behind? And here also let everyone inquire how it is with them with respect to envy of others for their spiritual prosperity.9 [[You remember what was the spirit of Cain toward Abel, of the seed of the serpent toward the seed of the woman, of Ishmael toward Isaac, of the Jews toward Christ, of the elder brother toward the prodigal. Beware that you cherish not their spirit, but rather rejoice in the good estate of others as much as if it were your own.]]

[II. Of exhortation.] [[The subject also exhorts us to disallow and put away everything approaching to an envious spirit. So contrary is the spirit of envy to a Christian spirit, so evil in itself and so injurious to others, that it should be disallowed and put away by all, and especially by those who profess to be Christians. Great numbers cherish the hope that this is their character, and that they have been endued with a new spirit, even the spirit of Christ. Let it then be evident to all that such is your spirit by the exercise of that charity that envieth not. In the language of the apostle James, James 3:13–16, "Who is a wise man, and endued with knowledge among you? Let him show, out of a good conversation, his works with meekness of wisdom. But if ye have bitter envying and strife in your hearts, glory not, and lie not against the truth. This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish; for where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work." The spirit of envy is the very contrary of the spirit of heaven, where all rejoice in the happiness of others; and it is the very spirit of hell itself, which is a most hateful spirit,1 and one that feeds itself on the ruin of the prosperity and happiness of others, on which account some have compared envious persons to caterpillars which delight most in devouring the most flourishing trees and plants.

[[And as an envious disposition is most hateful in itself, so it is most uncomfortable and uneasy to its possessor. As it is the disposition of the devil and partakes of his likeness, so it is the disposition of hell and partakes of its misery. In the strong language of Solomon, Proverbs 14:30, "A sound heart is the life of the flesh, but envy is the rottenness of the bones." It is like a powerful eating cancer, preying on the vitals, offensive

-- 231 --

and full of corruption. And it is the most foolish kind of self-injury; for the envious make themselves trouble most needlessly, being uncomfortable only because of others' prosperity, when that prosperity does not injure themselves, or diminish their enjoyments and blessings. But they are not willing to enjoy what they have because others are enjoying also. Let, then, the consideration of the foolishness, the baseness, the infamy of so wicked a spirit, cause us to abhor it, and to shun its excuses, and earnestly to seek the spirit of Christian love, that excellent spirit of divine charity which will lead us always to rejoice in the welfare of others and which will fill our own hearts with happiness. This love "is of God," 1 John 4:7; and he that dwelleth in it, "dwelleth in God, and God in him," 1 John 4:16.]]

-- 232 --

SERMON SIX: A CHRISTIAN SPIRIT IS A HUMBLE SPIRIT
Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly. I CORINTHIANS 13:4–5.

IN the preceding part of the fourth verse, the Apostle shows the nature and tendency of Christian charity or love with respect to evil received from others, and doing good to others in these words, "charity suffereth long and is kind." In the latter part of the verse, he shows the nature and tendency of charity with respect to good possessed by others, and by ourselves.
