3. The Spirit influences the minds of men primarily in two ways: by operating on them and by dwelling in them. The former is "common" to natural men and to saints. "Legal humiliation" is an example of "the mind's being assisted to a greater sense of... the natural perfections of God, such as his greatness, terrible majesty, etc." An example of the Spirit's dwelling in the minds of the saints is the "sense... given in evangelical humiliation, by a discovery of the beauty of God's holiness and moral perfection" (Affections, p. 311. Ed. italics). ↩
4. About two lines blank in the Andover copy. Insert from TE, p. 42. ↩
5. The Treatise on Grace lists "common grace, common illuminations and common affections" as influences that are "of the nature of the Spirit" but that do not make us "spiritual persons" (Grosart, Unpublished Writings, p. 42). In Sermon Fourteen below JE's concentration is on the common ordinary influences of the Spirit that have yet to pass away. There he lists "common convictions of sin, common illuminations, common religious[!] affections." In the present sermon he is concerned chiefly with the common extraordinary gifts that have already passed away. ↩
6. The copyist first wrote "peculiar"; then crossed it out, and wrote "special" above the line. Two possible explanations for this (and like instances below) are: (1) he realized he made a mistake in transcription, his eye having lighted upon the word "peculiar" later in the sentence; or (2) "peculiar" was in JE's booklet in both places, and the copyist decided upon a bit of editing to avoid the repetition. Most likely, his was an error in transcription, which he then corrected. See text below, at n. 7, for another use of "special" for "saving" or "uncommon." ↩
7. The Application of JE's sermon Distinguishing Marks drew this same distinction between the "ordinary gracious" and the extraordinary influences of the Spirit that may be "common"; "a man may have those extraordinary gifts and yet be abominable to God." Balaam, Saul, and Judas are mentioned, then Matthew 7:22, as above (Works, 4, 278–79). ↩
8. Here at the end of JE's eloquent tribute to the great privilege it was for men of old to be "endued" with the extraordinary gifts listed by St. Paul, attention should be called to the meaning the word "extraordinary" has when used in Distinguishing Marks (1741) and Affections (1746). In the context of JE's interpretation of revival phenomena, "extraordinary" means unexpected, strange, unusual, out-of-the-ordinary. That is all the word could mean, since it was JE's view that real supernatural "extraordinary gifts" had ceased seventeen centuries before. JE's discrimination, among strange or unusual revival phenomena, was between those occurrences that are "no certain signs" [Affections, Pt. II) in contrast to twelve "Distinguishing Signs" (Pt. III) of truly gracious affections. And in Distinguishing Marks, his language was "what are not signs that we are to judge of a work by"; indeed, he used a double negative, i.e., "what are no evidences that a work wrought amongst a people, is not the work of the Spirit of God" (Distinguishing Marks, p. 228. Ed. italics). ↩
9. The Andover copy reads: "I come now in the III Place to show...," with "III" on the left margin. Subsequent similar transitions to new par. numbers will be regularly edited as here. ↩
1. Here, and at "his ordinary influences" in the next sentence, the copyist changed references to the Holy Spirit to "himself" and "his." These words are written over "itself" and "its," faintly discernible. "It" and "itself" were used before this point. Eight uses of the more personal pronouns follow immediately in the paragraph. ↩
2. The First and Second points above— that saving grace is inherent in the nature of him that has it, and that in the ordinary gift of graced affections the Holy Spirit communicates himself as a vital principle, and not his effects alone— can be supplemented by Affections, especially in the First, Fourth, and Seventh Distinguishing Signs. There also JE mentions some of the same unusual phenomena, as in the sermon, that are "no certain signs." See n. 8 above. From the side of the human subject "participation" is at the center of JE's theology, here and in End of Creation. ↩
3. See Sermon One, p. 133, n. 1. JE distinguished between the "natural" and the "spiritual" images of God. The latter is "the amiable image and likeness of Christ" (just below). He also speaks of the "blessed image of God" in those who have the "ordinary gracious influences" of the Spirit. (Distinguishing Marks, pp. 278–79.) See also Freedom of the Will, ed. Paul Ramsey, in Works, 1, 166 and n., and Affections, Pt. III, Third Sign, esp. p. 256. ↩
4. Here in Andover and at the following insertion there are blanks that could each be filled with a single word. I judge none to be needed in the first instance. TE (p. 54) reads: "influencing us to holy and heavenly lives." ↩
5. Here in Andover is a break of about three-fourths of a line. TE simply omits the words "He foretold many things." Because these words concerning Balaam seem to be needed, I place a period after "things" and suggest that nothing more need be said. This conveys a crispness like the references to prophecy that follow. The absence of terminal punctuation, however, and the fact that three-fourths of a line is blank in the copy at this point, may indicate that JE drew a line to remind himself to recite some of the things Balaam foretold. ↩
6. At about this place TE (p. 56) proceeds to point Fifth. ↩
7. JE's sense is: Hence we may argue from the infinitely superior excellence of the fruits or effects of the ordinary gifts over those of the extraordinary— since grace is saving, extraordinary gifts are not. ↩
8. The end or purpose for which extraordinary gifts were given is more fully elaborated in Sermon Fourteen. There, too, as in Distinguishing Marks, pp. 280–81, JE classed such gifts as "childish" things. ↩
9. Miscell. no. 379 (c. 1728–29): "That extraordinary and miraculous way was made use of once, only for the introducing of the more perfect way. This is the endof the other way; it is excellent in itself; but inspiration and miracles are good for nothing without it... Seeing the end is come, it would be impertinent to continue the means" (Ed. italics). JE cites the final verse of 1 Corinthians 12 and the first verse of 1 Corinthians 13 in support of his view. But extraordinary outpourings were both necessary, pertinent, and suitable in the transitus from the Jews, the church of old, to "the gospel state of the church, which is not any particular enclosure but is dispersed throughout the whole world." ↩
1. From here to the end of this point Eighth, TE deletes and replaces far more than was needed to deal with the final page of this section in the original sermon booklet, of which Andover was a faithful reproduction. Evidently TE, writing in the nineteenth century, had little interest in the thoughts that JE was wrestling with from the verses in Hebrews. In its entirety TE's replacement (pp. 60–61) reads:
They were instructed in Christianity, and through the common influences of the Spirit they received the word with joy, like those in Matt, xiii. 20; and withal received the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit; "were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, tasted of the heavenly gift, and the powers of the world to come"; spake with tongues; prophesied in Christ's name; and in his name cast out devils; and yet after all, openly renounced Christianity; joined to call Christ an imposter, as his murderers did; and so "crucified to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to open shame." Of these it is that the Apostle says: "It is impossible to renew them again to repentance." Such apostates, in their renouncing Christianity, must ascribe the miraculous powers which themselves had possessed to the devil. So their case became hopeless; and their condemnation must be exceedingly aggravated. And from this it appears that saving grace is of infinitely more worth and excellence, than the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit.
Then follows point Ninth, below. ↩
2. At this point Andover leaves about four and one-half lines blank. This was doubtless its equivalent for the long dashes in the sermon booklet by which JE reminded himself to summarize what he had previously said. The words I venture to insert, here and below, are from JE's "Notes on the Bible" in Sereno E. Dwight, The Works of President Edwards: With a Memoir of His Life. 10 vols. (New York, 1829–30), 9, 538–41. To fathom the meaning of Hebrews 6:4–6, JE reads the passage in the light of Acts 19:2–6 (the doctrine of baptisms), Matthew 13:18–23, with Luke 8:18 (the parable of the sower— which he correctly understood as a parable of the soils) and Numbers 22 (the story of Balaam's disobedience). In the same context, JE interpreted Hebrews 10:25–29 to mean the sin against the Holy Ghost, whose type in the Hebrew Bible was the presumptuous, willful sabbath breaker in Numbers 15:32–36. The source of the standard Puritan sermon on Hebrews 6:4–6 and the sin against the Holy Ghost was Calvin, Institutes, III, iii, 21–24. ↩
3. Ver. Acts 19:2 continues: "And they said unto him, We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost." Then, after comparison with John's baptism, "When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them and they spake with tongues and prophesied" (ver. Acts 19:5–6). Numerous entries in the "Miscellanies" combine these verses with those mentioned in the previous note in interpreting the meaning of the sin against the Holy Ghost. ↩
4. Nearly two blank lines in Andover. ↩
5. One-fourth line omitted, to the right of the page; then the same space on the next line on the left of the page. ↩
6. Space for one or two words, on left of page. ↩
7. Space for one, perhaps two, words in the middle of the line. Assuming the copyist faithfully represented the page in the sermon booklet, the location of words on the page has no great significance. JE simply set down these incomplete sentences where best to catch his eye, with dashes to indicate he was to extemporize. At the end of this sermon there likely was another such page. But there I use the third Bellamy fragment in construing the best text. See App. I, editorial comments on fourth example. ↩
8. "But he that receiveth the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it. Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while; for when tribulation and persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended," Matthew 13:20–21. ↩
9. Ten lines blank. JE clearly intended to summarize and apply the story in Numbers 22–24 about how Balaam at first obeyed the word of the Lord not to go with the emissaries of Balak but later disobeyed and accompanied them. TE's reconstruction of the paragraph (see above, p. 163, n. 1) not only ignores the reference to Balaam but adds statements not implied in the copy-text or in JE's notes on these biblical passages, e.g., that those who received common graces and then apostatize "must ascribe the miraculous powers which themselves had possessed to the devil" (TE, p. 61). ↩
1. I judge that JE's extemporized interpretation of the Hebrews passage would have been something like my text above. The difficulty in the way of the present-day reader is largely theological. Indeed it is intellectually difficult to understand how, on JE's view, it was possible to commit the sin against the Holy Ghost in Northampton seventeen centuries after the extraordinary gifts had passed away. See App. V. ↩
2. See below, Sermon Fourteen, whose text I inserted above. ↩
3. Full line blank in the copy. TE (p. 62) has JE repeat the Doctrine (abbreviated). Surely the preacher did so here. But the space in Andover was likely in the original booklet. ↩
4. The copy has no terminal punctuation after "unless," which is followed by three-fourths of a line blank. TE (p. 62) reads: "bestowed on such, in any age of the world, the apostolic age excepted." ↩
5. These words occur on a stray slip of paper in the Andover collection. The handwriting is that of the copyist. They obviously belong here, where there is a full line blank with no terminal punctuation after "Solomon." ↩
6. This is the language of Affections, Pt. II. Here, however, JE is arguing that even if they were real, extraordinary gifts would be no "sure signs of saving grace" because, when they were, such gifts were "common." ↩
7. The foregoing concise list of supposed evidences was given lengthy analysis by JE ten years later in his May 1748 sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13— especially under that sermon's second and third uses, of self-examination and of warning, comprising most of the third preaching unit. The warning is "not to give heed to any pretended revelation in yourself or others" (MS l.69va). Experiences looked upon as of a "spiritual nature" are to be tested "whether or no they ben't such as suppose immediate revelation" (MS l.47va). Moved to preach against the excesses to which the Great Awakening led, with "wild" claims "all over the country" (MS l. 48ra) to Scripture— free inspiration, JE wrote (consistent with the charity series): "If there be any such revelation as those in these days they are not spiritual. They were not spiritual in the days when there were such things. There was then a vast difference between those things and the saving operations" (MS l.5ora). Transcribed for me by Stephen D. Crocco. The sermon booklet is not paginated. See p. 83, n. 5 above. I refer to this important sermon below in my notes to the present sermon and to Sermons Nine, Fourteen, and Fifteen. ↩
8. The Andover copyist mistakenly transcribed "desiring." TE (p. 66) reads: "And the only way, therefore, in which any can know their good estate, is by discerning the exercises of this divine charity in their hearts, for without charity, let men have what gifts you please, they are nothing." He then proceeds immediately to point Third. ↩
9. Space for only one line in the copy. For my insert, cf. above, n. 8. ↩
1. Here JE grants that God "often does direct persons' thoughts to such and such scripture... to stir up the exercises of grace." This means the grace they have. Cf. his view that "secondary beauty" has "a tendency to assist those whose hearts are under the influence of a truly virtuous temper, to... enliven in them a sense of spiritual beauty" (True Virtue, p. 565 below, and Intro., p. 36). In Affections he stresses also a reverse influence, that truly gracious affections often stir up unusual experiences that are "no certain signs." Two remarkable and connected Miscellanies, no. 123. SPIRITUAL SIGHT and no. 126. SPIRITUAL UNDERSTANDING OF THE SCRIPTURES (c. 1724), bear upon the issue here, giving as they do a sort of Lockean explanation of the phenomena in question.
"When upon an occasion I was more than ordinarily affected with the passingness of one generation after another," JE writes in No. 126, "how that all those who made such a noise and bluster now, and were so much concerned about their life, would be clean gone off from the face of the earth in sixty or seventy years' time, and that the world would be left desolate with respect to them, and that another generation would come on, that would be very little concerned about them, and so one after another; it was particularly affecting to me, to think that the earth still remained the same through all those changes upon the surface, the same spots of ground, the same mountains and valleys where those things were done, remaining just as they were, though the actions were ceased and the actors quite gone— and then this text came into my mind," i.e., the text "One generation passeth away, and another cometh; but the earth abideth forever" (Ecclesiastes 1:4) that in "a common frame of mind, seemed insipid," and its final words a non sequitur.
"Hence we learn," a corollary tells us, "how places of Scripture are often suddenly brought into mind, which are almost forgotten perhaps, before; the motions that are then in the mind being so exactly agreeable thereto, that if there be any footsteps of it in the memory, it will bring them before the mind. So that the Spirit of God don't immediately suggest the places to us, as though by inspiration, but by stirring up correspondent affections of mind, whereby the mind is naturally put in mind of the text that is so agreeable to it; as much as one speech or sentence puts us in mind of another like it, or as one instrument of music answers of itself to another in harmony and concord." ↩
2. Romans 11:25–26, "Blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved." ↩
3. By "Antichrist" JE meant the Roman apostasy. And cf: "It appears to me much more probably that God should give immediate revelations to his saints in the dark days of popery, than now in the approach of the most glorious and perfect state of his church on earth" (Distinguishing Marks, p. 281). ↩
4. No space in Andover copy. ↩
5. In his 1748 sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13 JE frames an objection on behalf of "some wild people of late," namely, "that in times past God has given no new revelation since the apostles' times; yet he may do it now, being about to introduce a new dispensation" (MS l.31va— b). But he replies, "God don't remove one dispensation to make way for another unless it be better" (MS l.32vb– 33ra), or without a change of ordinances. No such new dispensation is to be expected (MS l.36rb). This discussion is introduced between the fifth and sixth arguments for the first inference under the first use of information. That inference, comprising the whole of the sermon's second preaching occasion, reads: "Hence we may learn that it is not to be expected that any of those gifts that imply divine revelation should be suffered in these days because the canon of Scripture has been complete, the church of God completely furnished with a standing rule of faith and practice, and means of grace all settled and established; and therefore the great end of all these gifts is abolished" (MS l.15vb). Transcribed by Stephen D. Crocco.
In JE's alphabetical Table to the "Miscellanies" there are five listings in which there is reference to this May 1748 sermon, one a duplicate. These are under: "Canon: of the Scripture, complete"; "Dispensation: no new one to be introduced, see sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13 (first inference, fifth argument in answer to the objection there)"; "Gifts of the Spirit, extraordinary, have ceased"; "Revelations: immediate, not given in these days"; and "Scripture: the canon finished." By contrast, there is but one reference in the Table to the 1738 sermon scries, to Sermon Thirteen, under "Perseverance, see sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:7." There is a second unlisted reference, to Sermon Fourteen, tucked away in Miscell. no. 756.
The 1748 sermon, and citations of it in the Table, show JE's growing insistence on the foregoing topics a decade after their comparatively abbreviated treatment in 1738 in Sermons Two and Fourteen. No doubt JE preached many times on texts from 1 Corinthians 13, marking for revision and reusing the 1738 booklets, now missing. The 1748 sermon is the only evidence we have of his composition of a fresh sermon on a verse or verses from this chapter. See also my notes to Sermons Nine, Fourteen, and Fifteen. ↩
6. A fragment of Bellamy's part-copy begins at this point, and continues on into Sermon Three. See App. I. ↩
7. Here— and to the end of Sermon Two— I adopt the text of the third fragment of Bellamy's copy into the text of this edition. For explanation of the editorial problem, see App. I, fourth example. ↩
8. TE (p. 69) adds after "his own blood," where there is no break in the copy, "and to glorify the Holy Spirit who hath sealed it to their souls." Thus TE composed a trinitarian formulation. In these sermons JE speaks simply of our duties to God and Christ. ↩
9. TE concludes the sermon with a "use of exhortation." This was not announced in the copy, unless by the Roman numeral "I" preceding "Use may be of instruction" above, to which there is no corresponding "II" in the copy. Clearly Bellamy came to an end; moreover, his tone had already become that of an exhortation. Consistent with electing his ending, I deleted the "I" at the beginning of the Improvement. TE's exhortation and the sentences immediately preceding his replacement for "lies with," read as follows:
how little this divine love hath wrought in your heart to incline you to live for God and Christ, and for the extension of his kingdom? O! how should such as you show your sense of your high privileges, by the exercises of love; love that is manifest toward God in obedience, submission, reverence, cheerfulness, joy and hope, and toward your neighbor, in meekness, sympathy, humility, charitableness, and doing good to all as you have opportunity. Finally,
5. The subject exhorts all unrenewed persons, those who are strangers to this grace, to seek this most excellent blessing/or themselves. Consider how miserable you now are while wholly destitute of this love, far from righteousness, in love with the vanities of the world, and full of enmity against God. How will you endure when he shall deal with you according to what you are, coming forth in anger as your enemy, and executing his fierce wrath against you. Consider, too, that you are capable of this love; and Christ is able and willing to bestow it; and multitudes have obtained it, and been blessed in it. God is seeking your love, and you are under unspeakable obligation to render it. The Spirit of God has been poured out wonderfully here. Multitudes have been converted. Scarcely a family has been passed by. In almost every household some have been made nobles, kings, and priests unto God, sons and daughters of the Lord Almighty! What manner of persons, then, ought all of us to be, how holy, serious, just, humble, charitable, devoted in God's service, and faithful to our fellowmen. As individuals and as a people, God has most richly blessed us, and as both individuals and a people, it becomes us to be a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people, showing forth the praises of him that hath called us all out of darkness into his marvellous light! "Now consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear you in pieces and there be none to deliver. Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me, and to him that ordereth his conversation aright, will I show the salvation of God!" [Psalms 50:22–23] ↩
1. I have broken JE's rather long sentence by inserting a semicolon after "circumstances." Nevertheless, there remains grammatical disagreement between "a person's disentangling himself" and "their" purse. Bellamy remedied this by replacing "were such as called for," etc., with a new sentence: "For such was the state of things that some were called to give up all things, and entirely disentangle themselves from the cares and cumbers of worldly possessions," etc. On the short title I give to this sermon, see App. I. ↩
2. The fragment of Bellamy's part-copy ends at this point, with the catchword "second" indicated as the first word of the next, missing page. ↩
3. Andover copy reads "there." ↩
4. See nn. 8 and 9 below for the meaning of the word "sincerity." ↩
5. The verse in Acts begins: "Neither is worshiped..." JE frequently changed words within quotations— from Scripture or from other writings— to elide with his text. This is cited as an example; similar occurrences will not be noted. ↩
6. TE (p. 84) proceeds immediately to Reason 2. ↩
7. Archaic usage meaning deception, trickery, a false statement or a lie. The Oxford English Dictionary (hereafter O. E. D.) illustrates: "the Folly of younge Men and the Fallacies of Women" (1641), "the Fallacies of Sense" (1654), "the fallacy of human friendship" (1837). ↩
8. In Christian ethics in general and in Puritan piety and self-scrutiny in particular there is a strong tendency towards a morality of inward intention. The use of the word "sincerity" in the Doctrine and throughout this sermon— together with JE's use of the word "kindness" for "cheerfully and freely doing good to others" in Sermon Four, and the argument in Sermon One that "reason teaches that whatever performances or seeming virtues there are without love are insincere and hypocritical" (p. 137 above, Ed. italics)— manifest this impulse toward a gesinnungs Ethik. As a corrective JE taught both a doctrine of natural and infused virtues as well as the moral rule of Scripture. Norman Fiering affirms that "hypocrisy" did not have our meaning of the deliberate deception of others; a hypocrite was rather someone mainly self-deceived. (Moral Philosophy at Seventeenth Century Harvard [Chapel Hill, Univ. of North Carolina Press, 1981], p. 172). Granting this, JE's discussion of the mixture of sincerity and hypocrisy remaining in the heart (the seat of both) shows that he did not expect "purity of heart" in this life. The "little sincerity" acceptable to God means that the Christian life was always in via toward holiness. ↩
9. This sentence announce four things that belong to sincerity in the heart. The copy treats only two: truth and freedom. TE completes the list with integrity and purity, under his use for self-examination. He also has uses of conviction and of exhortation.
For JE on the ambiguity of "sincere endeavors," on direct and indirect willing of a thing, on sincerity as the reality of will and endeavor (vs. pretense) and on "virtuous sincerity," see Freedom of the Will, pp. 312–19; and the section on sincerity in Miscell. no. 1153. MORAL INABILITY FREEWILL. SELF-DETERMINING POWER (a lengthy entry composed not long after his dismissal from the church in Northampton, and marked for use or when used at that place in Freedom of the Will).
JE uses but one of the alternative meanings of sincere or sincerity that O. E. D. lists. See Intro., p. 61, n. 8. ↩
1. Half-line blank in Andover copy. TE (p. 90) deletes "of," which seems to begin an iteration. ↩
2. Andover reads "evangelical." On balance, the theological context does not favor TE's "filial" (p. 90). ↩
3. Here the copy ends. TE (pp. 90–92) goes on to complete the list of four things belonging to the nature of sincerity, which were announced. See above, n. 9. ↩
4. On this point, see Sermon Twelve on the "concatenation" of the virtues or graces of a "proportionate Christian." ↩
5. Having spoken of the third and fourth things that belong to sincerity in the heart, TE proceeds (pp. 92–95) to add a use of conviction and a use of exhortation. TE's ending, as noted above, is needed to complete the copy on the elements in the nature of sincerity. Andover's use of self-examination is numbered "I"; this suggests at least another use to come. Hence I complete the sermon by including TE's entire ending. ↩
1. This sermon was delivered in three "preaching units." The first covered the first point of doctrine; the second, improvement of that doctrine, with objections and answers; the third introduced the second point of doctrine, with its application. Evidently it was important to JE to hold in even balance the two dispositions mentioned in the text to which love inclines: suffering long and being kind. Even under the first point, JE shows (pp. 189–90 below) the nature of "long-suffering" to be gentleness and kindness; it is not merely endurance under ills suffered but endurance in well-doing with love in the heart. Therefore, he states one doctrine, divided into two heads. Because of its organization into I. Doctrine/Application and II. Doctrine/Application, the sermon may be described as duplex. In the short title given it, I endeavor to suggest the evenhandedness, indeed the singularity, of the doctrine JE meant to convey. TE divided the sermon into two, the second part being the third preaching unit. For this reason, this edition of Charity prints fifteen sermons, one fewer than TE's "Lectures." Not only does the form of the Puritan sermon indicate the correctness of my editorial decision. There is additional support for this decision in the fact that the entire duplex sermon was copied in one booklet (no. 4), the text forty-four pages in length, numbered in sequence. Only the final sermon, preached on two occasions, approaches this length (forty-three pages, also a single booklet, no. 15). ↩
2. The verse continues: "gentleness, goodness, faith." Obviously either JE or the copyist stopped quoting with the fruit that was the theme. In the next citation of this same list of "fruits of the Spirit," one more word is quoted from the verse, i.e., "gentleness," which again fits the context exactly. See text below, at n. 4. ↩
3. TE omits any reference to taverns, a well-known occasion for some of the friction between JE and the church in Northampton. His sentence (p. 99) reads: "Other ways of injury are abundant; but the amount of injury by evil-speaking of this kind is beyond account." ↩
4. See above, n. 2. Here "gentleness" is a specific qualification of meekness, whose meaning is further characterized in this section. In Affections "meekness" is listed among those "lamblike, dovelike" qualities of Jesus Christ that "may by way of eminence be called the Christian spirit"; the "little children" of Matthew 19:14 are its model as well as those animal types. Such meekness and the virtue of meekness spoken of in the sermon may seem, on a careful reading, to have little in common. But then in Affections, JE himself frames an objection that lamblike, dovelike, and childlike meekness seems not fit for the Christian's warfare, and is incompatible with the virtue of "Christian fortitude." In showing that there is no inconsistency, JE discovers steadfastness and boldness to belong to the strength of the meek (Eighth Sign, pp. 344–45, 349–52), even as here in the sermon there is kindness and gentleness in the strength of the long-suffering of the meek. Early in the improvement (the second preaching unit below), the movement is from Christ's "lamblike quietness of spirit" to a composure that will fit us to live in a world such as this, with Christian imperturbability and "greatness of soul." ↩
5. My conjecture is that TE wanted to lessen the vividness of JE's language. He reads (p. 106): "We should not only control our passions when we are injured, and refrain from giving vent" (Ed. italics). ↩
6. Two-word blank in the copy. TE (p. 107) has no sentence parallel with this one, so he read "excitement" instead of "rustle" in the preceding sentence. ↩
7. Andover reads "firm." But the imagery is of wind and the surface of water, not of a house built firmly on rock. So here I follow TE (p. 106), consistent with Andover's "rustle" (n. 6 above). ↩
8. TE (p. 109) reads "censurable." ↩
9. With the words "what wickedness," without final punctuation, the copy comes to four and one-half blank lines. ↩
1. My reconstruction of the text— largely from TE (p. 112)— maintains Andover's rhetorical repetitions: "If we consider the wickedness there is in the world..."; "And if we consider the goodness of God to some particular populous cities..."; "And especially if we consider God's long-suffering towards his elect..." ↩
2. TE's "see the hand of God" (p. 116) seemed initially the better reading. "Eye the hand of God" was also strange to any of the other Edwards scholars I consulted. The accuracy of the Andover copyist was supported, however, by two texts: (1) Esther Edwards Burr wrote to her mother after Aaron Burr's death, "I hope God has helped me to eye his hand, in this awful dispensation" (The Journal of Esther Edwards Burr, 1754–1757, ed. Carol F. Karlsen and Laurie Crumpacker [New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 1984], p. 294; and in Sereno E. Dwight, The Life of President Edwards, in Works, 1, 567. Ed. italics), and (2) JE himself wrote "the Eye of the soul" and "The soul shall be as it were all eye to behold and yet all act to love" (Ed. italics), in his remarks on the "Beatifical vision" in his 1735 sermon on Romans 2:10. See App. III, pp. 723–26 below. ↩

7. Here ends the first preaching unit; the second gives the application of the first point of doctrine. An example may be given at this point of JE's summary transitions to a second preaching unit within the same sermon form. He begins by restating the duplex doctrine: "A Christian spirit disposes persons meekly to bear ill that is received from others, and cheerfully and freely to do good to others. / I. We have shown how a Christian spirit disposes persons meekly to bear ill that is received from others, or the injuries that others do them. / First. We took notice of the various kinds of injuries which persons suffer from others. / Second. What is meant by meekly bearing such injuries. / Third. How that love that is the sum of the Christian spirit will dispose men to do thus. I come now to make some brief/ IMPROVEMENT." These introductory words in the copy are omitted from the text above. So also the briefer recapitulations below, at the beginning of the third preaching unit of the present sermon, and similar summaries in Sermons Six, Seven, Ten, and Fifteen— each of which required two preaching occasions to complete. ↩

5. End of the second preaching unit. Andover's transition to the third preaching unit represents JE as simply repeating the same duplex doctrine announced at the beginning and in the introduction to the second preaching unit. TE made what follows in the text into a separate (and fifth) lecture.
TE does not have Andover's detailed enumeration of answers to the final objections above, which probably reflects the sermon booklet's brief reminders of topics to extemporize. Still, the words with which TE concludes his fourth lecture (pp. 138–39) are roughly parallel to Andover's ans. to obj. 2 and 3. TE quotes from Romans 12:19 only the words, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord"; and then completes his fourth lecture, going beyond the copy-text to say:
He interposed wonderfully for David, as he has for very many of his saints; and if you do but obey him, he will take part with you against all that rise up against you. And in observation and experience of men, it is generally found, that a meek and long-suffering spirit puts an end to injuries, while a revengeful spirit does but provoke them. Cherish, then, the spirit of long-suffering, meekness and forbearance, and you shall possess your soul in patience and happiness, and none shall be permitted to harm you more than God in wisdom and kindness may permit.
The third and final preaching unit, below, completes the sermon by taking up the second point of doctrine, with its Application.
The word "kind"— and "kindness"— in JE's exposition is, of course, drawn from the King James version of the text. "Kindness" or "lovingkindness" was also one translation of Hebrew chesed in the Old Testament; "mercy" was another. Kindness as a virtue, a fruit of agape or chesed, may be compared with the kindness of the "instinctual kind affections" discussed in True Virtue, Ch. VI. Evidently the quality of kindness expounded in the sermon is referred to later by JE as "true virtue" "mixing its influence with the natural principle," guiding and regulating its operation, or alternatively as a quality excited or infused by a holy love operating alone. See below, pp. 616–18. ↩

5. Below in the text at n. 6, TE has an extended reference to Haman's envy of Mordecai (concluding with a reference to Joseph and his brothers), which has no parallel in the Andover copy. Therefore I call attention that at this point TE (p. 163) has the following single sentence: "And Joseph's brethren, we are told, Gen. xxviii. II, envied him when they had heard his dream, which implied that his parents and brethren were yet to bow down before him, and that he was to have power over him." Here the disposition is envy; in TE's later use of the Joseph story, this envy turns into dislike and hatred of persons. ↩
6. From this point on, for two full pages, TE (pp. 164–66) is only roughly parallel to the Andover copy, down to their common reference to Joseph's brethren, just before Doctrine II. A number of sentences are alike in both, but TE interweaves an extended account of Haman's envy of Mordecai (Esther 5:13). The text above, beginning at this point, may be compared with TE's version:
He is very much of the spirit of Haman, who in view of all "the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all the things wherein the king had promoted him," still could say (Esther v. Esther 5:13), "Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting in the king's gate." From such a spirit, the envious person stands ready to rejoice at anything that happens to diminish the honor and comfort of others. He is glad to see them brought down and will even study how to lower their estate, as Haman did how to humble and bring down Mordecai. And often, like Haman, he will show his uneasiness not only by planning and scheming, but by actual endeavors of one kind or another to bring them down; and the very first opportunity of pulling them down that offers, he will gladly embrace. And it is from this disposition that the sight even of others' prosperity often sets the envious on talking against them and speaking evil of them, even when perhaps they do not know them. Envying them the prominence they have obtained, they hope by speaking evil of them in some measure to diminish their honors, and lower them in the esteem of men. This suggests, again,
2. That the opposition of the envious to the prosperity of others will be manifest in a dislike of their persons for it. Seeing how others prosper, and what honors they attain, the envious dislike, and even hate them, on account of their honor and prosperity. They entertain and cherish an evil spirit toward them, for no other reason but that they are prospered. They are embittered against them in spirit only because they are eminent in name or fortune. Thus Haman, it is said (Esther v. Esther 5:9), "was full of indignation against Mordecai" because he saw him "in the king's gate," and because "he stood not up, nor moved for him"; and Joseph's brethren (Genesis xxxvii. Genesis 37:4, Genesis 37:5), "hated him and could not speak peaceably unto him," because his father loved him; and when he had dreamed a dream implying their inferiority, "they hated him yet the more." And so the envious generally resent the prosperity of others and their coming to honor, as if in it they were guilty of some injury to themselves. Sometimes there is a settled hatred toward others upon this account, leading as in the case of Joseph's brethren (Genesis xxxvii. Genesis 37:19–28), to acts of the greatest cruelty and wickedness.

2. The words quoted are ver. 1 Timothy 6:4. This suffices for the needed moral "precept." Ver. 1 Timothy 6:5 and 1 Timothy 6:6, if spoken, would weaken the conceptual and rhetorical force of the sermon. ↩
3. Under "how... the doctrines and history of the gospel hold forth to enforce those precepts" against envy in Scripture, JE develops the moral notions of "grudging" (or "begrudging") and "grudging not." These notions are extensively deployed in the next sermon on humility, and in Sermon Fifteen. In face of Philippians 2:8, JE denied that "humility" was a virtue of "the divine nature" of Christ; "grudging not" is the proper notion, as the text above says. Not only did the devil envy or "begrudge" man's happy state in Eden. JE also believed those angels who fell did so not so much from towering pride, but from that vice in their hearts in the form of envy or grudging, when they learned that God had determined to raise human creatures below them in creation to a higher destiny than theirs in glory, i.e., to the highest honor and blessedness in union with himself. On these angels' envy of the hypostatic union, see Intro., p. 75, n. 9.
In fact, JE's notion of pride was not the simple one of storming heaven's battlements to usurp God's throne. His was a subtler concept, essentially that of a "comparative spirit." That is, pride is born of a creature's vulnerability to perceived threats to his dignity, not of inordinate strength or uncomplicated assurance. "Pride don't consist most essentially in a too high conceit of oneself, but in a disposition inordinately to affect our own comparative dignity" (Miscell. no. 747. SELF-RIGHTEOUSNESS PRIDE [roughly contemporary with the charity sermons. Ed. italics]). "Pride may be thus defined. It is that habit or state of a person's heart whereby he is inordinately disposed to exaltation amongst other beings as to his comparative dignity or worthiness of esteem and value.. /.. The immediate object of pride is not... a man's own excellency considered absolutely. 'Tis not a disposition in a person to seek his own excellency absolutely, or a disposition to be excellent. A man can't excessively affect his own excellency... he can't excessively desire to be excellent, to have those qualifications that will render him a just object of esteem... 'Tis only a comparative dignity that pride affects, or the height that one is in or may be conceived to be amongst other beings. Nor is it the love and esteem of others absolutely considered... It don't content pride to be esteemed and loved by others, and to be so much valued by them, but to be highly valued and esteemed comparatively. 'Tis a person's comparative exaltation [among superiors, equals or inferiors]... whether those other beings with whom we compare our exaltation or dignity be God or creatures" (Miscell. no. 95O. PRIDE. HUMILIATION [c. 1744]). ↩

Another possibility cannot be excluded, however, namely, that when preaching this sermon on a subsequent occasion JE himself wrote in the Haman example, and that the copyist chose to transcribe only the original sermon, leaving to Dwight the decision whether or not to include the clearly marked later passages. ↩

1. JE's language here reflects that of the "bid prayers" written out by members of the church in Northampton. The following example is typical: "Ebenez Clark Junr and his wife desire the prayers of this Congregation that god wold Sanctifie his Holy afflicting hand to them in takeing away his Sister martha Russell of Sunderland by death..." See Stephen J. Stein, "‘For Their Spiritual Good’: The Northampton, Massachusetts, Prayer Bids of the 1730s and 1740s," William and Mary Quarterly 3d ser. 37 (1980), pp. 261–85, no. 30 on p. 274. Stein's article is a study of all the prayer bids which— because of the cost of paper JE saved, sewed into his sermon booklets or other notebooks, and used, writing in the margins or on the reverse side. ↩

4. Here ends the first preaching unit. In this instance the copy contains no summary or connecting sentences; instead, it simply restates the text and the two points of doctrine and passes to the second point. ↩
5. On its face, JE applies to the Day of Judgment a verse that might better be read as referring to God's ruling and judgment in history: "The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed with desolation, and the hands of the people of the land shall be troubled: I will do unto them after their way, and according to their deserts will I judge them; and they shall know that I am the Lord." Nevertheless, this is another instance of JE's accurately choosing his precept from a verse, bearing in mind the tradition of figural interpretation of Scripture. Historical judgment was seen as a type of the final Judgment. ↩
6. Cf. Affections, pp. 311–40. This Sixth Sign of gracious affections may be the most subtle discussion of humility as a Christian virtue that JE ever wrote, in its intermingling of analysis of pride throughout. The sermon on humility, however, is purer and, it may be, more powerful in the following respects: (1) The sign lacks the sermon's affirmation of humility as an essential qualification of love, implied in it; and (2) the sign sets up the correlation, "legal humiliation: God's greatness:: evangelical humiliation: God's beauty and holiness," while in the sermon the divine love that implies humility is a love to God also "as an infinite superior," i.e., humility is a creature excellence related both to God's greatness and to his holiness. This sermon, more than the Sixth Sign, prepares the reader to understand the words in End of Creation, Ch. I, Sec. I, p. 423 below: "so that the degree of regard should always be in a proportion compounded of the proportion of existence and proportion of excellence, or according to the degree of greatness and goodness considered conjunctly." Also to understand the account of the spiritual beauty in moral agents in True Virtue, Ch. I, p. 548 below, to the effect that "the degree of the amiableness or valuableness of true virtue, primarily consisting in consent and a benevolent propensity of heart to Being in general... is not in the simple proportion of the degree of benevolent affection seen, but in a proportion compounded of the greatness of the benevolent being, or the degree of being and the degree of benevolence." This consent to Being in itself or benevolent propensity of heart to Being in general is identified in the next chapter as love to God. So, it can be suggested, true virtue tends to humility as an effect and also implies humility as an essential qualification, as JE says of divine love in this sermon. Humility's sense of comparative meanness is founded in the heart's sense of the aweful greatness and the beauty or holiness of God. The same is true of other virtues as well, both later in the sermon series and in the dissertation, since the sum, principle, and source of them all is charity. ↩

To examine ourselves." ↩
3. See n. 2 above. No space before use of exhortation. After the quotation of Hab 2:4, TE's parallel (p. 222) expands the use of examination:
and the fact that "God resisteth the proud" (James IV. James 4:6) or, as in the original, "sets himself in battle array against him," shows how he abhors a proud spirit. And it is not every show and appearance of humility that will stand the test of the gospel. There are various imitations of it that fall short of the reality. Some put on an affected humility; others have a natural low-spiritedness, and are wanting in manliness of character; others are melancholy or despondent; others under the convictions of conscience by which, for the time, they are depressed, seem broken in spirit; others seem greatly abased while in adversity and affliction, or have a natural melting of the heart under the common illuminations of the truth; to others there is a counterfeit kind of humility, wrought by the delusions of Satan: and all of these may be mistaken for true humility. Examine yourself, then, and see what is the nature of your humility, whether it be of these superficial kinds, or whether it be indeed wrought by the Holy Spirit in your hearts; and do not rest satisfied, till you find that the spirit and behavior of those whom the gospel accounts humble, are yours. ↩

It should be noted, however, that TE's second exhortation is rather indistinguishable from the first hortatory use. ↩
1. JE held this view from his mid-twenties, when he wrote in his "Miscellanies":
The best philosophy that I have met with of original sin and all sinful inclinations, habits and principles is undoubtedly that of Mr. Stoddard's of this town of Northampton: that is, that it is self-love in conjunction with the absence of the image and love of God; that natural and necessary inclination that man has to his own benefit, together with the absence of original righteousness; or in other words, the absence of that influence of God's Spirit, whereby love to God and to holiness is kept up to that degree, that this other inclination is always kept in its due subordination. But this being gone, his self-love governs alone; and having not this superior principle to regulate it, breaks out into all manner of exorbitancies, and becomes in innumerable cases a vile and odious disposition, and causes thousands of unlovely and hateful actions. There is nothing new put into the nature that we call sin, but only the same self-love that necessarily belongs to the nature working and influencing, without regulation from that superior principle that primitively belongs to our nature, and that is necessary in order to the harmonious existing of it. This natural and necessary inclination to ourselves without that governor and guide will certainly without anything else produce, or rather will become, all those sinful inclinations which are in the corrupted nature of man.
Then JE observes that all the exercises and actings of the powers and inclinations in the souls of men, whatever they be, are but God's continual and immediate influence. Such, indeed, was his understanding of every physical being or motion in the world of nature: these are from an immediate operation of God without which there would be nothing. So it seemed entirely reasonable to suppose that a moral inclination (such as self-love)
is nothing but God's influencing the soul according to a certain law of nature; therefore the influence that upholds one inclination being withdrawn, and God continuing the same influence to the upholding of the other inclination, according to the former rule and method, according to that law which we call the law of nature, it naturally and of itself breaks out into all those exorbitances. It might easily be shown how this will unavoidably, without any new infusion, produce all those inclinations that we call pride, covetousness, lasciviousness, malice, envy, etc. [Miscell. no. 301. SIN AND ORIGINAL SIN (c. 1727–28]
This sermon speaks mainly of the natural self-love of the creature (which is as necessary to human nature as a faculty of will is) left alone, without original righteousness to regulate and channel it, and of the work of the Spirit in restoring that spiritual image of God. But if in 1738 JE believed anything like the principles of common morality and the "laws of nature" governing the ordinary dispositions and behavior of men (not to mention "common" grace) set forth in True Virtue, Chs. III, then he must also have believed that self-love is never left alone between the Fall and the redemption which God is working in every age. Many entries in his notebooks, e.g., on conscience, attest that JE treated "self-love" and "selfishness" in one or another of these contexts. See App. II. ↩

See above, Sermon One, p. 132, n. 8. ↩

The notion of "placing" one's happiness (and its related concept of finding or "looking on" others' happiness as one's own)— elaborated in the present sermon— was first introduced in the sermon "Long-Suffering and Kindness": "[F]or the more men love God, the more they will place all their happiness in God; they will look on God as their all, and this happiness and portion is what men cannot touch" (Sermon Four, pp. 195–96 above, with n. 6). These concepts are important not only for an understanding of the sermon series (e.g., Sermons Twelve and Fifteen) but for a proper understanding of End of Creation and True Virtue as well. ↩
1. Love of complacence: to place one's happiness in good found and to be enjoyed in others. Love of benevolence: to place one's happiness in good to be enjoyed by others. 9. Note the tension in this sermon between knowing persons' qualities and states by their fruits and reserving to God the judging infallibly concerning those states of soul; between this sermon and the next on holy practices; and by way of emphasis throughout JE's writings. Among the marks or signs of gracious affections, the "certainter" the sign, the less public it is. Nevertheless, greatest stress on openness to human judgment is to be found in the Twelfth Sign. Having shown that Christian practice is "a great and distinguishing sign," JE writes, "I may go further, and assert, that it is the chief of all the signs of grace, both as evidence of the sincerity of professors unto others, and also to their own consciences" (Affections, p. 406. Ed. italics). See Intro., pp. 82–83.
The contrary pole was exhibited in JE's 1748 sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13. He began this lengthy sermon on the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit by defining them as "those that consisted in or implied inspiration or immediate revelation" (MS l.1rb); and from this drew his second inference under use of instruction, third preaching occasion: "Hence we may learn that there are none in these days [that] have a gift of discerning and certainly knowing who are true Christians" (MS l.44ra). "It is evident," JE wrote, "that this can't be known by men certainly any other wise than by immediate revelation, because God only knows of himself by his own discerning. / Nothing is more plain than that the knowing the gracious sincerity and the insincerity of professors of godliness is spoken of in Scripture as the divine prerogative" (MS l.44ra-b). "And therefore if any know, it must be because God tells him or immediately makes it known to him. A gift of discerning the saving influences is as much revelation as a gift of discerning of spirits. Men of themselves see nothing but the outward appearance" (MS l.44vb). That such revelation is not now to be expected— or claimed— "further appears" because God has "directed us to judge by other means. / Fruits. Faith is known by its fruits" (MS l.46va). "Some would argue from hence that persons may certainly know, [lacuna in MS] But the word don't imply certain knowledge, but only that men shall know and distinguish by this rule, as shall ordinarily be fitter for our own safety" (MS l.46vb— 47ra). "'Tis God's prerogative to judge infallibly according to men's works. But then these persons [whom JE opposes] don't pretend to know this way. [They know] others by their sheep's clothing or by immediate revelation" (MS l.47ra-b). JE lists as "delusive" the following ways of knowing spiritual states: an unaccountable perception that their minds are suddenly possessed with what they can give no reason for, that such a thing will come to pass, having a strong idea of some fear, of Hell flames and time in them, "Sees 'em dead. Sees in his imagination streams of lightning and fire from heaven. Sees 'em with faces shining. That God has some favor or respect to them... by something like a vision. Hearing singing" (MS l.50va— 52vb). Even when read in course, scriptures "don't declare in particular. And therefore when persons suppose that scriptures came to them to declare to them in particular, they are deluded." So any and all particular declarations of salvation or damnation suppose "a new revelation and is to add to the Scriptures" (MS l.57ra). See above, Sermon Two, p. 169, n. 7. Additional references to this important sermon are in the notes to Sermons Fourteen and Fifteen. ↩

The interpretation of ver. 1 Corinthians 13:6 as a summary of all holy practices is more emphatically insisted upon in Sermon Eleven, text explication 2 (pp. 313–16), and Sermon Twelve, text explications 1 and 2 (pp. 326–27). The Treatise on Grace (Grosart, Unpublished Writings, p. 33n.) suggests the same division as the sermon: the Apostle "had plainly summed up all parts of charity towards our neighbor in the 6th verse." The fruits of divine love in sermons following this tenth have respect more to God than to our neighbors, though one and the same principle of love in the heart goes out to both. ↩

Later on JE supports his interpretation by reference to the biblical use of the word "know," which, says he, means practical knowledge as opposed to speculative (Doctrine I, Fourth, pp. 296–97 below). The idea of "doing the truth" or "truth to be done" or obeyed (JE's "veracity or faithfulness") is most clear in the Johannine literature. Thus JE cited "walkest in the truth" from III John, ver. 3 John 3, in explicating the text above. Also cf. JE on William Wollaston, in True Virtue below, p. 570, and n. 1. ↩

The distinction did not allow separation; for, as JE wrote, "The act of the soul, and the exercise of grace, that is exerted in the performance of a good work, is the good work itself, so far as the soul is concerned in it, or so far as it is the soul's good work" (ibid., p. 423. Ed. italics). In contemporary language, JE held neither a morality of intention nor a morality of action; his ethics was neither wholly motive analysis nor wholly action analysis. ↩

Particular graces are not to be distinguished from particular Christian graces; all these subheads are on the same level. Curiously, Andover (or JE) begins a new sequence of numbers, with 4 for the next point. I change this to "Sixth," and so on through "Twelfth." TE subordinates some to other of these points in both preaching units. ↩
1. The O. E. D. defines contemn to mean to slight, or treat as of small value, with contemptuous disregard, or with contempt. JE invokes, of course, the stronger of these meanings in this context. By contrast, condemn means to pronounce an adverse judgment. In this sermon on holy practices it is significant that of the two, JE chose "contemn." For all his stress on holy practices, he understood their holiness to spring from the disposition of moral agents. Cf. p. 298 above, n. 6. Another use of "contemn" is to be found in Sermon Twelve below, p. 337, at n. 3. Later TE avoids the word, and here he reads "condemn" (p. 343). Psalms 10:13; Psalms 15:4; Psalms 107:11; Canticles 8:10; Isaiah 16:14; and Ezekiel 21:10, Ezekiel 21:13 are instances in the King James version of the use of to "contemn" meaning to despise or loathe. ↩

1. According to TE, JE quoted or recalled words from the Old Testament that refer to God: "For I am the Lord your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy." The nearest equivalent in the New Testament is Matthew 5:48: "Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father in heaven is perfect"— words of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount. Why, then, would JE use the verse from Leviticus to refer to being like Christ? Two explanations may be suggested. First, that JE's usage was an instance of typological interpretation: the veiled meaning of the Old Testament verse is unveiled and made manifest in Christ. Second, that JE believed that throughout Scripture, what is said of the one supreme God is said also of Jesus Christ. See Miscell. no. 1358. DIVINITY OF CHRIST; and App. III, pp. 719–20 below. ↩

5. TE (p. 389) formulates the doctrine as "That the graces of Christianity are all connected together and mutually dependent on each other"; and the short title he gives to this lecture is "All the Graces of Christianity Connected." Throughout his text TE avoids using "concatenated." Yet "concatenated" was not and is not an archaic word, though perhaps it is more rarely used now than in previous centuries. A catena is a chain or connected series. If the prefix con— added only the meaning of connected together, then JE's usage "concatenated together" would be tautologous. The prefix con— does more, however; the meaning is "altogether, completely, intensely linked together." Perhaps this was another way of saying of faith, hope, and love in this sermon, with one word, what JE says of charity and humility in Sermon Six and affirms of all the virtues in perfection in heaven (Sermon Fifteen): these graces are of the same essence and imply one another.
It is reasonable to conjecture that TE edited to simplify JE's language. Not so Alexander B. Grosart, in editing Unpublished Writings. At a significant point at the beginning of ch. II of Treatise on Grace Grosart printed: "And thus it is that there is a consentanation∗ of graces. Not only is one grace in some way allied to another, and so tends to help and promote one another, but one is implied in the other" (p. 30. Ed. italics. Grosart's second sentence above outlines the three points under Doctrine I of the present sermon). Grosart simply could not read JE's hand. The asterisk directs the reader to a note, which reads: "Query, = harmony, i.e., from consentaneous?— G." Here surely JE's cardinal word "consent" came to Grosart's mind as he tried to make out how JE might have used one word to mean "a consenting together." That word likely was "concatenation." But JE uses "consentaneous" in Miscell. nos. 89 and 197. In No. 89. JUSTICE (c. 1723–24), he shows that God "can have no desire of being unjust for his own interest" from the nature of excellency, or being's consent to entity, which "must necessarily be consentaneous or agreeable to perceiving being, and the contrary, contradiction or dissent to entity, must be disagreeable to it" (Ed. italics). In No. 197. CHRISTIAN RELIGION (c. 1725), JE wrote that "it seems to me exceeding congruous, and in the highest manner consentaneous, that God, a being of infinite goodness and love," who created the world to make the creature happy in his love, "should give to the creature the highest sort of evidence or expression of love" (Ed. italics). ↩

The concatenation of all Christian graces expounded in this first point of doctrine is expressed by JE in Affections as the "beautiful symmetry and proportion" among affections that are truly gracious and holy (Tenth Sign, pp. 365–76). Religious affections show themselves counterfeit by their "monstrous disproportion" or "great partiality" (ibid., p. 365), their "strange partiality and disproportion" (ibid., p. 367). Compare the monster image in connection with the new birth in the present sermon's first use for instruction, below in the text at n. 5, p. 334. Also, the very last sentence of the sermon uses the same striking simile used in Affections, p. 365, in discussing the contrary of this Tenth Sign: "Ephraim is a cake not turned,’ Hosea 7:8, half roasted and half raw: there is commonly no manner of uniformity in their affections." A beautiful symmetry and uniformity— the concatenation of all the graces— is the "aesthetic" element in JE's understanding of the Christian moral life. ↩

That is, the graces of the Christian life— the "virtues"— are specifications of divine love in the heart, not variously denominated excellencies of the faculties of the human soul. But compare this account of true virtue(s) with True Virtue, pp. 616–18 below. ↩

9. An early Miscellany expressed this concatenation-theme as follows: "The graces of the Spirit, especially those that more directly respect God and another world, are so nearly allied that they include one another; and where there is the exercise of one, there is something of the other exercised with it: like strings in concert, if one is struck, others sound with it; or like links in a chain, if one is drawn, others follow. So that humiliation that there is in repentance, implies a principle of faith, and not only so, but something of the exercise too; so that a person according to the gospel may be in a state of salvation, before a distinct and express act of faith in the sufficiency and suitableness of Christ as a Savior. Persons are justified upon the first appearance of a principle of faith in the soul by any of the soul's acts: but a principle of faith appears and shows itself by the exercise of true repentance and evangelical humiliation; for the graces are all the same in principle, especially those that more respect God and Christ and another world" (Miscell. no. 393. HUMILIATION [c. 1729]). The point argued in this Miscellany is that "'tis not fairly argued... that the first act of grace is always faith (though ordinarily I believe it is) any otherwise than as faith is implied in the acts of other graces"; or, put positively, "there is an exercise of faith in humiliation," i.e., an exercise of faith may be implicit in what is, manifestly, only an explicit exercise of the soul in evangelical humiliation. This thesis JE explored, against Solomon Stoddard— in the year of the latter's death— who held that there was no grace in humiliation and that the first gracious act that ever was exerted must be an explicit act of faith. JE further states that, since all graces are concatenated together, the need for repentance of sin "don't infer, that the first act of grace shall be an explicit act of repentance of that sin" (Ed. italics). ↩

This may be in men while natural men. The other is a having the heart drawn off by being shown something better, whereby the heart is really turned from it. So in like manner, there is a twofold bringing a man off from his own righteousness. One is being beat or forced off by convictions of conscience. Thus, there can be a false and a true "mortification" both of moral pride and of covetousness toward worldly things. 1. To get this reading out of the Greek πάντα ὑπομένει, Edwards separates the prefix ὑπο from μένει. Long before the New Testament was written the prefix had merged with the substantive, as for example in our word "withstand." To "endure under" is the meaning, just as we today might make a point by saying that to "withstand" has great strength because it means to "stand with." JE was quite aware of the unusual exegesis he was giving, whether his claim was that "remains under all things" is a more "liberal" translation (Andover) or "if literally translated" (TE, p. 411). Likely, the word in the sermon booklet could be read either way. In Miscell. no. 750. perseverance (contemporaneous with the charity sermons) JE wrote, "Grace shall endure all things, and shall remain under all things, as the expression πάντα ὑπομένει literally signifies in 1 Corinthians 13:7" (Ed. italics).
The importance theologically of the perseverance— the preservation— of the saints is signaled by the fact that the present sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:7 is the only sermon in the 1738 series referred to in JE's alphabetical Table to the "Miscellanies," under "Perseverance." ↩

8. TE (p. 420) changes this word to "prevails." Clearly, this was a mistake; "prevent" derives from the Latin praevenire "to go before." In traditional usage, the word meant "to go before to aid." By a strange twist, nineteenth-and twentieth-century usage has come to mean "to go before to stop." O. E. D. defines the archaic theological usage to mean "to go before with spiritual guidance and help; said of God, or of his grace anticipating human action and need." We can speculate that it was the loss from common understanding of the providential, optimistic meaning of the word that allowed its neutral meaning more and more to assume a negative connotation. In the text above, of course, JE is speaking of an unmortified "principle" of sin in the heart in the case of false grace, going before to overwhelm any tendency to good in natural men when they are tried. Cf. JE's view of the Fall, Sermon Seven above, p. 252, n. 1. ↩

Seeing the end is come, it would be impertinent still to continue the means." ↩

MILLENNIUM must have been composed after the present sermon, preached in October 1738. JE cited his "serm. on 1 Corinthians 13:8 1st Inference" in answer to the question, "Whether or no the miraculous gifts of the Spirit of God will be restored then?" The "inference" mentioned is almost certainly point First of the Application above. This reference to the 1738 sermon series is discoverable only by looking in JE's alphabetical Table for "756" under "Millennium," along with some thirteen other numbers. The only explicit reference to Charity in the Table is to Sermon Thirteen, under the entry "Perseverance: see sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:7." ↩
8. TE (p. 457) has no parallel to "and faith fail." The faith here in question is that listed among the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit in 1 Corinthians 12, not the "common temporary faith" that fails when the saints come to die because there is no charity in it. JE used the expression "the faith of miracles" in the text explication of Sermon Two, consistent with the words, "Though I had all faith, so that I could remove mountains," 1 Corinthians 13:2. The notion of a faith that is only "common" was first introduced in the sermon series in Sermon Ten above, p. 299, text at n. 7. ↩
9. Before proceeding to the next paragraph, TE (p. 458) expands upon the infancy-maturity analogy: "They are adapted to the childish state of the church, while holy love is more to be expected in its full grown and manly state; and in themselves they are childish, in comparison with that holy love which will so abound in the church when it comes to its perfect stature in Christ Jesus [Ephesians 4:13]." JE quotes this verse from Ephesians earlier in the sermon; when joined with 1 Corinthians 13:11, it is central to his theme— meriting, it would seem, more than the brief treatment given above and two references to it below in the text explication of Sermon Fifteen.
This childhood-manhood figure is elevated to the Doctrine of the 1748 sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13: "The extraordinary influences of the Spirit of God imparting immediate revelations to men were designed only for a temporary continuance while the church was in its minority, and never were intended to be statedly upheld in the Christian church" (MS l.4vb). But since there is a figural correspondence between "the kingdom Christ is building up in the soul" and the kingdom he is building up in the world, there is no significant alteration in JE's exposition in the 1748 sermon from that of the sermon series. The later sermon is actually a more forceful and lengthy assault upon claims to immediate revelation and "spiritualism" among extremists in the aftermath of the Great Awakening. Moses foretold, the prophets foretold, the last of them before he had finished foretold, the Baptist foretold further revelation to come. Jesus Christ also foretold further revelation of the mind and will of God in the days of the Apostles (MS l.16va— 20vb; John 16:12–13 and John 17:18–19).
But the Apostles did not in that sense foretell; the last of them closed the canon of Scripture (Revelation 22:18).
Of the extraordinary gifts, "the end of 'em was not to amuse the world" (MS l.11vb), but completely to furnish the church with "a standing rule of faith and practice and means of grace all settled and established, and therefore the great end of these gifts is abolished" (MS l.15vb, Application I, under the first inference of the use of instruction, second preaching unit). Then the church passed from its childhood to its manhood.
JE uses minority-majority as a type. So, figurally consistent with the church's majority in this world since the first century, JE can at the same time interpret 1 Corinthians 13:12 to mean that particular members come to full manhood only in heaven, where there is no need of any means of grace and the "common ordinary" influences of the Spirit also have ceased (MS l.2va-b, text explication. Transcribed by Stephen D. Crocco. Numerical references are to leaves in the booklet; a and b refer to the vertical columns on each leaf.) Similar correspondences are a key to understanding the twofold "perfect" and the twofold "imperfect" states of the church, and the twofold "failings" of gifts in the text explication of Sermon Fifteen. ↩

2. TE's text (p. 459) reads "kindling." ↩
3. See above, n. 1. ↩
4. "Thus having a standing rule God has given for general use, it [Scripture] becomes an ordinary means of knowledge /... that is not so properly to be said to be a common way" (1748 sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13, MS l.6rb— 6va, under the first point of doctrine. Ed. italics). So in JE's use of terms, Scripture, like divine love, gracious affection, or sense of the heart, is an "ordinary" but "uncommon" way to God's mind and holy will. ↩

6. This qualification is a hypothetical contrary to fact. In a similar vein, JE gave— as the sixth argument for the inference that "it is not to be expected that any of these gifts that imply divine revelation should be suffered in these days"— the fact that "a gift of working miracles has not been revived" (1748) sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13, first inference under the use of instruction, requiring the entire second preaching occasion to deliver. MS l.15vb and 1.36va.
By defining extraordinary gifts in this later sermon as those that "consisted in or implied inspiration or immediate revelation," JE separated prophecy, inspiration, tongues, and interpreting tongues from the gift of working miracles. (The last is not mentioned in the text, ver. 1 Corinthians 13:8–13; it is listed in 1 Corinthians 12:8–10 and in 1 Corinthians 13:2). JE's language is to say that the "end" of extraordinary gifts, in that sense, was to "settle" a standing revelation and to "impart" to the church a standing rule and ordinances. His language for the "end" of miracles is to establish and confirm that revelation of the will and mind of God (MS l.13vb— 14ra and l.15ra). JE's terminology in Sermons Two and Fourteen is entirely consistent with this, only more compact. The gift of miracles was, as it were, a means confirming the (other) extraordinary gifts, whose end, in turn, having been accomplished, all have ceased.
The "immediate revelation" JE rejects as no more to be expected or "suffered" means "God's making known some truth by immediate suggestion of or to the mind without its being made known by sense of reason or by former revelation" (MS l.5rb). JE heaped argument upon argument on such claimants. E. g., "'Tis an easy thing for a man to say that he has divine revelation made to him in his mind, which is out of other persons' view." (MS l.39va, answering an objection introduced between the fifth and the final sixth argument for the first inference of the use of instruction, second preaching unit.)
It was in this direction that, some say, New England transcendentalism took Edwards' views. This may be so, if the sense of the heart is decoupled from Scripture; if JE's natural types are entirely separated from their scriptural antitypes; and if the kingdom of Christ building up in the soul is decoupled from the kingdom of Christ building up in the world in the work of redemption. ↩

1. For an evaluation of the rhetorical power of this sermon, see Intro., p. 61, with n. 7. ↩
2. The expression "latter ages" refers to a first "maturity" of the church in the coming reign of Christ on earth. TE abbreviates the final clause of this sentence to read, "or of comparative earthly perfection" (Ed. italics). JE evidently is adumbrating the more detailed account of millennial events in the sermon series preached the following year on the history of redemption. ↩
3. One may ask whether "latter ages" was not the expression here, as in Andover at n. 2 above. TE's word is "latter" at this point, but "later" at n. 2. ↩
4. JE uses childhood-maturity as a natural type-antitype (one affirmed by St. Paul). Thus, the "imperfect" of the church in its New Testament state: the "perfect" of the church in the latter ages:: the failing of extraordinary gifts with the closing of the canon: the failing of all common influences of the Spirit with the end of the militant state of the church, following the great apostasy at the end of the latter ages, i.e., the ceasing of all gifts except charity from the church in heaven. The "twofold failing" is of (1) "common extraordinary" gifts since the closing of the canon of Scripture and the death of the apostle John, and of (2) "common ordinary" gifts, ordinances, and means of grace upon the death of particular saints and, from the church collectively, at the end of the world. The first of these failings corresponds to that (more) perfect state of the church in this world since the apostolic age. Since then, and for all time, the "ordinary, uncommon" work of the Spirit is gracious affection or divine love in heart and life. The second failing corresponds to individuals' or the church's passage from all time of earthly trial to triumph in heaven. See above, Sermon Fourteen, p. 355, n. 8; p. 362, n. 8 and n. 9; p. 364, n. 6. Always JE's view was progressive. ↩
5. Ver. 1 Corinthians 13:12. Although the text announced was ver. 1 Corinthians 13:8–10, JE no more limits himself strictly to these verses than in the 1748 sermon that returned to these verses under the text ver. 1 Corinthians 13:8–13, i.e., to the end of the chapter. ↩
6. The question, In what sense will divine love be "as it were, the only gift or fruit of the Spirit" in heaven? has no simple answer. How JE conceived "the unity of the virtues" in perfection is summed up in his notions of essential implication, concatenation, and participation, analyzed in detail in my Intro. JE's 1748 sermon is puzzling on this point. He began the second preaching unit by announcing that "faith and hope don't abide in heaven in the sense in which the Apostle commonly uses the terms," citing and probably delivering 2 Corinthians 5:7, compared with 2 Corinthians 4:18, Hebrews 11:1, Hebrews 11:9–10, Hebrews 11:13, and Romans 8:24–25 (MS l.15rb). According to this sermon, the Apostle says faith, hope, charity, these three, abide "when the church in some sense shall have become adult at a time when prophecy and tongues shall have ceased and vanished away. But this will not be when the church is come to be adult in the sense in which it will be in heaven" (MSl.11ra-b). Does this mean that the three virtues "abide" in the "adult" state of the church between the apostolic age and the end of the world? Does that then suggest that greater unity among the virtues will be the final perfection of the righteous? ↩
