1. The reference is to Jesus' words, Matthew 19:29 or Mark 10:29–30. Sermon Fifteen is remarkable in that it omits discussion of the reunion of family members and friends as one of heaven's attractions. JE treated this expectation elsewhere, without the sentimentality TE's nineteenth-century edition introduces at this point.
In Miscell. no. 639. HEAVEN (c. i 733), JE directly raised the question, "Whether the saints when they go to heaven have any special comfort in their meeting with those that were their godly friends on earth?" He answers that indeed there will be special comfort in again meeting "godly friends," more than from seeing other saints they had only heard of. "Neither do I see how it argues infirmity," JE continued, "for a saint in glory to have a special respect to another, because God made use of him as an instrument to bring him into being, and so is the remote occasion of his eternal blessedness, or because he himself was the occasion of bringing the other into being or that the same agreeableness of tempers that is the foundation of special friendship here, may be so also in another world." The entry concludes with the injunction: "This should move us to lay religion and virtue in the foundation of all our friendships, and to strive that the love we have to our friends be a virtuous love, duly subordinated to divine love. For so far as it is so it will last forever. Death don't put an end to such friendship, nor can it put an end to such friends' enjoyment of each other."
Such subordination may seem austere. It is, however, entirely consistent with "pure benevolence" mixing its influence— in this world— with natural principles to guide and direct them, in the familial love examples in True Virtue, Ch. VII, pp. 617–18 below. Cf. also the words which JE, when dying, asked his daughter to deliver to his wife, Sarah: "Give my kindest love to my dear wife, and tell her, that the uncommon union, which has so long subsisted between us, has been of such a nature, as, I trust, is spiritual, and therefore will continue forever" (Dwight, Life, p. 578).
TE was apparently troubled by JE's decision not to portray family reunions in heaven. His version (pp. 474–75) of the conclusion of point Third, down to Doctrine III, reads as follows:
All the truly great and good, all the pure and holy and excellent from this world, and it may be from every part of the universe, are constantly tending toward heaven. As the streams tend to the ocean, so all these are tending to the great ocean of infinite purity and bliss. The progress of time does but bear them on to its blessedness; and us, if we are holy, to be united to them there. Every gem which death rudely tears away from us here is a glorious jewel forever shining there; every Christian friend that goes before us from this world is a ransomed spirit waiting to welcome us in heaven. There will be the infant of days that we have lost below, through grace to be found above; there the Christian father, and mother, and wife, and child, and friend, with whom we shall renew the holy fellowship of the saints, which was interrupted by death here, but shall be commenced again in the upper sanctuary, and then shall never end. There we shall have company with the patriarchs and fathers and saints of the Old and New Testaments, and those of whom the world was not worthy, with whom on earth we were only conversant by faith. And there, above all, we shall enjoy and dwell with God the Father, whom we have loved with all our hearts on earth, and with Jesus Christ our beloved Savior, who has always been to us the chief among ten thousands and altogether lovely, and with the Holy Ghost our Sanctifier, and Guide, and Comforter; and shall be filled with all the fullness of the Godhead forever! ↩
2. I adopt TE's reading, p. 476. One could as well say "freely and infinitely" or "unchangeably and infinitely," since the necessity in question was a moral, not a natural, necessity. ↩
3. As earlier defined (Sermon Four, p. 213, n. 2; and Sermon Seven, p. 257, n. 1), love of benevolence means to will and love the good to be enjoyed by another. The context above suggests that love of complacence (to will and love the good in another) is also perfected in heaven; that, indeed, the familiar distinction between these loves is transcended and abrogated among the hosts of heaven. ↩
4. Here ends the first preaching unit. The fifth and sixth main points of doctrine remain to be expounded, before the application. Everything essential to the perfect peace and love, above, among the hierarchies of holiness in heaven was formulated by JE when he was twenty years of age in Miscell. no. 5. HEAVEN (c. 1723). Cf. also corol. 2 to Miscell. no. 681 (c. 1736), one of whose titles is DEGREES OF GLORY. On growth in glory, see App. III. ↩
5. TE's word (p. 488) seems needed to replace Andover's "mirror." I should point out, however, that in his "Miscellanies" JE tried first one way and then another to express the perfect communication in heaven. See passages quoted in Intro., p. 96, n. 3. For example, Miscell. no. 188. HEAVEN (early in his tutorship at Yale, 1724–25): "The best, most beautiful, and most perfect way that we have of expressing a sweet concord of mind to each other, is by music. When I would form in my mind an idea of a society in the highest degree happy, I think of them as expressing their love, their joy, and the inward concord and harmony and spiritual beauty of their souls by sweetly singing to each other. But if in heaven minds will have an immediate view of one another's dispositions without any such intermediate expression, how much sweeter will it [be]. But to me 'tis probable that the glorified saints, after they have again received their bodies, will have ways of expressing the concord of their minds by some other emanations than sounds, of which we cannot conceive, that will be vastly more proportionate, harmonious and delightful than the nature of sounds is capable of; and the music they will make, will be in a medium capable of modulations in an infinitely more nice, exact and fine proportion than our gross air, and with organs as much more adapted to such proportions." Communication is the obvious key to understanding the meaning of "emanation" here and in End of Creation as well. ↩
6. On grace perfecting nature or love perfecting (actualizing) the natural virtues in JE, see Intro., pp. 55–59. The "wisdom and discretion" mentioned here, as also "prudence" implied on p. 371 above, at n. 9, are surely similar to the "virtuous conscientiousness, or a sanctified conscience" listed in True Virtue, Ch. VII, p. 617 below. ↩
7. Cf. Miscell. no. 263. HEAVEN (c. 1727): "If the saints after the resurrection shall see by light, and speak and hear by sounds, 'tis probable that the medium will be infinitely finer, and more adapted to a distant and exact representation... The organ also will be immensely more exquisitely perceptive... So the eye may be so much more sensible, and the medium (the rays) so much more exquisite, that for aught we know, they may distinctly see the beauty of one another's countenances and smiles, and hold a delightful and most intimate conversation, at a thousand miles' distance." ↩
8. This seventh point under Doctrine V concerning the "excellent circumstances" of the love in heaven was formulated in Miscell. no. 741. HAPPINESS OF HEAVEN (shortly before the sermon series) by a remarkable combination of the language of "looked on" and "not begrudging" with the language of "propriety" and "theirs." See Intro., p. 101, n. 5. The reader may ponder the possible equivalence of propriety in one another with the goal of the primary propensity or union of heart to Being itself simply considered. Cf. JE's "‘absolute Benevolence’ (if I may so call it)" in True Virtue, Ch. I, p. 544, which is excited by "a propensity and union of heart to Being simply considered" (the primary object of virtuous love). ↩
9. Cf. love of one's own happiness and "placing," or finding, one's own happiness in that of another. And see above, n. 3, p. 375, on the coincidence of love of benevolence and love of complacence when these loves are perfected in heaven. ↩
1. This tenth and last point under Doctrine V concerning the "excellent circumstances" of the expression and enjoyment of love in heaven is JE's equivalent to Augustine's argument that the summum bonum must also be immutabile. The good that entirely satisfies the human heart must not only be the highest of all goods in rank of perfection. It must also, Augustine believed, be "something which cannot be lost against the will. For no one," he reasoned, "can feel confident regarding a good which he knows can be taken from him, although he wishes to keep and cherish it. But if a man feels no confidence regarding the good which he enjoys, how can he be happy while in fear of losing it?" (On the Morals of the Catholic Church, ch. III). Indeed, the higher the good the more sorrow, if it were a good that passes away, or a good we fear may pass away despite our heart's will and love of it. See App. Ill, pp. 715–16, for JE's similar statement on the saints' certain assurance of progress in the knowledge, love, and enjoyment of God and of one another. ↩
2. Before coming to the second point, TE's text (p. 501) continues: "And even if they are not confined to this society, but if any or all of them are at times sent on errands of duty or mercy to distant worlds, or employed, as some suppose them to be, as ministering spirits to friends in this world, they are still led by the influence of love to conduct, in all their behavior, in such a manner as is well pleasing to God, and thus conducive to their own and others' happiness." TE's rather romantic notion of the saints having the role usually ascribed to angels may be joined with his stress on cozy family reunions. See above, p. 383, n. 1. ↩
3. Or, less likely, "can," which Andover copied first, then corrected to "could." TE (p. 505) reads "could." JE's perspective upon the story of redemption is now, of course, that of looking back upon this world of trial. ↩
4. TE's parallel (p. 509) insures that the reader understands "this world" to mean heaven! ↩
5. Andover first copied, "in their hearts." Then seeing the words "Their hearts" beginning the next sentence, he reshaped his "their" to read "them" and crossed out "hearts." The passage reads quite well, however, with the repetition of "their hearts": once for JE's flame image, and again for soil. ↩
6. TE (p. 520) reads "danger." The rhetorical force of JE's account of hell as a place of hatred in his sermon on heaven as a "world," and a world of love (both contrasting with the present world of trial) will not escape a sensitive reader. Some, however, may need to be reminded that every great theologian (or poet like Dante) who believed literally in hellfire also gave a deeper, spiritual account of it. Cf. Luther's Sixteenth Thesis: "There seems to be the same difference between hell, purgatory, and heaven as between despair, uncertainty, and assurance." For Luther hell is complete despair, for JE hell is hatred, in as real a sense as it was fiery torment. ↩
7. TE, p. 523. Andover's "pass" is an error in transcription. ↩
8. Slightly more than a half-line blank, divided between two lines in the Andover copy. Insert from TE, p. 524. ↩
9. "Exhortation in two branches" was announced. Here Andover represents JE as turning point 5 of his list of "directions how to seek heaven" into the second exhortation. TE has none of this. His point 5 (pp. 528–30) extends to the end of the sermon. ↩
1. A lively hope is strangely not listed along with faith and love as one of the ways to heaven. Nor does the sermon imply that hope "abides" in heaven. This is quite consistent with the fact that in previous discourses JE treated the faith, hope, or love that are false or counterfeit as "common" influences that fail. Hope within heavenly perfection is correlated with progress there (App. III). Still, here again we face the question about the unity in plurality— the concatenation of virtues in perfection. See Intro., pp. 102–104, esp. p. 104, n. 5. ↩
2. TE's summary ending (pp. 529–30) parallels points 2 through 4 above: "Thus also you may have a sense of the glory of heavenly things, as of God, and Christ, and holiness; and your heart be disposed and opened by holy love to God, and by the spirit of peace and love to men, to a sense of the excellence and sweetness of all that is to be found in heaven. Thus shall the windows of heaven be, as it were, opened, so that its glorious light shall shine in upon your soul. Thus you may have the evidence of your fitness for that blessed world, and that you are actually on the way to its possession. And being thus made meet, through grace, for the inheritance of the saints in light, when a few more days shall have passed away, you shall be with them in their blessedness forever. Happy, thrice happy those who shall thus be found faithful to the end, and then shall be welcomed to the joy of their Lord! There they shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat, for the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and lead them to fountains of living waters, and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes!" ↩
